☆ How Architecture, Typology, and Adaptation Strategies Shape ASR for Low-Resource African Languages: A Controlled Empirical Study
Mercy Muchai, Kevin Chege, Nick Mumero Mwangi, Samuel Chege Maina, Felermino Ali, Elizabeth Ankrah, Ignatius Ezeani
Despite recent advancements in ASR, identifying effective architectures, fine-tuning approaches, and data adaptation strategies for low-resource languages remains challenging. We present a systematic comparison across five low-resource African languages and Swahili as a mid-resource contrast, fine-tuning three models from distinct architectures: Phi-4-multimodal-instruct, Whisper-large-v3-turbo, and MMS-1B-all. We analyze data sufficiency, monolingual versus multilingual adaptation, domain fine-tuning, and language-adapter transfer. Phi-4 achieves the best overall accuracy, MMS shows comparable CER, while Whisper exhibits high CER, consistent with known hallucinations and repetition loops. Performance saturates at different data scales, offering practical data-efficiency targets, while typological complexity consistently shapes error rates. Domain fine-tuning benefits Phi-4 and Whisper but degrades MMS, revealing limitations of adapter-based adaptation. Proxy language adapters outperform training MMS adapters from scratch.
☆ Efficient Agentic Audio-Visual Question Answering through Toolset Pruning and Modality Consolidation
Yi Wang, Tianzi Wang, Peter Bell
Fine-grained audio-visual question answering (AVQA) requires models to resolve complex cross-modal correspondences and temporally grounding from sparsely distributed evidence. Omni-modal agents, which autonomously orchestrate perception tools to actively collect evidence, achieve strong performance, but it remains unclear whether active perception from both audio and visual modalities depends on broad specialized toolsets, especially audio or visual modality-specific tools. Such systems may also introduce long execution trajectories and substantial inference cost. We investigate whether comparable performance can be retained with a compact workflow exposing only essential perceptual capabilities. Starting from the specialized-tool OmniAgent, we conduct staged controlled experiments that prune the toolset and progressively consolidate modality-specific tools into omni-modal tools, motivating a two-tool agent comprising only Omni-modal captioning and Omni-modal QA. Across three widely used AVQA benchmarks, our compact agent achieves comparable or better accuracy than the specialized-tool agent while reducing inference cost by around 70%.
☆ Structured Pruning of Feedback Delay Networks
Facundo Franchino, Karolina Prawda
Feedback delay networks (FDNs) are recursive filter structures used to synthesise artificial reverberation. Their feedback matrix governs both energy exchange between delay lines and the computation required at every sample, making its design central to balancing an FDN's acoustic performance and implementation efficiency. In this work, we develop an FDN-specific structured pruning method that connects these acoustic and computational concerns, allowing high-order dense orthogonal designs to be fitted to efficient implementations. The feedback matrix is replaced by stages of fixed permutations and small orthogonal blocks. We characterise connectivity growth with the network depth and derive exact conditional block updates for matrix fitting, followed by refinement against the reference FDN magnitude response. The resulting factors admit direct vectorised evaluation, with arithmetic cost and coefficient storage scaling linearly with network size for fixed block size and depth. On an Apple M2, the selected staged kernels achieve feedback-multiplication speedups over dense BLAS ranging from approximately threefold to over twentyfold across the tested network sizes, while substantially reducing coefficient storage. Objective metrics and listening tests indicate that the proposed staged approximations closely preserve the spectral and temporal character of their dense references. An analysis of processor utilisation and register reuse explains why execution time depends on more than the operation count. Finally, block size and depth provide practical control over response fidelity, storage, and real-time cost, allowing acoustic design to precede the choice of an efficient implementation.
comment: 11 pages, 8 figures, 4 tables. Submitted to the IEEE Open Journal of Signal Processing
☆ Streaming Speech Recognition on a Microcontroller: a 65.7M-Parameter Transducer in 2 and 4 Bits on the ESP32-P4
Billal Boumedine
We run Kroko, a 65.7M-parameter streaming Zipformer2 transducer for English, on the ESP32-P4, a microcontroller with two 400 MHz RISC-V cores, a 128-bit SIMD extension (PIE) and 32 MB of PSRAM, but no neural accelerator. Without any training, the encoder's 290 matrices are stored with 2 or 4 bits per weight in Hadamard-rotated groups: the width of each matrix comes from its measured sensitivity, and each matrix is first corrected toward the original model's output, then rounded with GPTQ and a search over the group norms. The released 71 MB of int8 weights become a 26.65 MB file. Activations are int16 between the matrix products and int8 into them. A C engine with hand-written PIE kernels processes each 1.28 s chunk of audio in 0.90 s on both cores, beam search included, and its PC build computes the same bits as the chip, so accuracy is measured on whole test sets. LibriSpeech WER is 4.34% on test-clean and 10.26% on test-other, against 3.94% and 9.17% for the released model; on FLEURS and Common Voice the gap grows to 2.3 and 1.1 points. A GPU simulator shows that the integer arithmetic costs nothing and that the whole gap comes from the weights, and an ablation on all of test-clean shows that GPTQ does most of the work. We also report the port's speed history, from 51.3 s to 0.62 s of encoder time per chunk, each design step measured again in one build, an attempt to reach 16 MB that stopped at 19.63 MB, and what did not work. We did not measure energy. The inference engine, the firmware and the 2/4-bit weights are available at https://github.com/BoumedineBillal/esp32-pie-asr.

☆ Personalising Parametric Audio Effect Recommendation for Vocals from Parameter-only Style Priors
Soumya Sai Vanka, Hayato Yamakawa, Kazunobu Kondo, Yu Takahashi, György Fazekas
Audio effect recommendation has mostly modelled style through reference audio and audio-domain losses. Because the parameter-to-audio map of parametric effects is many-to-one, such systems can match a reference without reflecting how a given engineer works. We instead model an engineer's style as a distribution over effect-chain parameters, which matches the data engineers can realistically share: console recalls store parameters without the audio they were applied to. Under a label-shift assumption, a personalised recommendation follows in closed form from a generic content model, a parameter population model and an engineer prior, with no paired engineer audio and no tuned weights. For vocal chains, the content signal is small but real, and concentrated in high-frequency EQ, dynamics and reverb. A forced-choice test with $14$ listeners found that the style-prior and content-only recommendations were distinguishable (89.3%), with results consistent with prior width affecting the balance between style and content, while parameter-space cosine does not predict perceived difference.
☆ Wav2Aug: A Drop-In Speech Augmentation Policy
Gianfranco Dumoulin Bertucci, Mirco Ravanelli
SpecAugment is the dominant speech augmentation policy, but researchers have studied it primarily for automatic speech recognition (ASR), and it operates on spectrograms, limiting its applicability to other speech tasks and waveform models. We propose Wav2Aug, a drop-in waveform augmentation policy that randomly samples two augmentations from a calibrated pool of waveform transformations. We calibrate the augmentation hyperparameters once and reuse them across tasks and architectures, eliminating task-specific tuning. Experiments on ten speech benchmarks show that Wav2Aug achieves ASR performance comparable to SpecAugment while improving over it on average across non-ASR tasks, yielding an average relative error reduction of 12.8% over the strongest compatible SpecAugment baseline. We further show that multi-view training provides additional gains, with two augmented views offering the best tradeoff between performance and computational cost.
☆ SelectSep: Target-Selective Video Queries for Audio Source Separation ICASSP 2027
Suyeon Lee, Doyeop Kwak, Joon Son Chung
Video-queried sound separation (VQSS) aims to isolate a target sound from an audio mixture using its corresponding video as a query. However, scene-level video queries can become ambiguous when multiple sounding objects are visible, particularly when the target and interferer are semantically similar. We propose SelectSep, a target-selective VQSS framework that jointly uses text and a single click coordinate to specify the target source and instance without requiring segmentation at inference time. We adapt the visual encoder through target-feature distillation with text and click conditioning, and then fine-tune the separator using the adapted visual features. We also introduce an on-screen interference setting, where both the target and interferer are visible, to evaluate target selectivity. Experiments on standard benchmarks and the on-screen interference setting demonstrate consistent improvements in separation quality and target selectivity, particularly for mixtures containing semantically similar sources.

☆ MiDiff: MIDI-Conditioned Diffusion Models for Drum Audio Enhancement
Elad Aspis, Sharon Gannot
Bridging the semantic gap between perfect symbolic musical structure and severely degraded acoustic signals offers a powerful paradigm for high-fidelity audio restoration. We introduce MiDiff, a diffusion-based generative model for drum audio enhancement that conditions the reverse process on temporally aligned Musical Instrument Digital Interface (MIDI) piano rolls. We extend the Score-Based Generative Models for Speech Enhancement (SGMSE) framework in the complex Short-Time Fourier Transform (STFT) domain by integrating a pretrained MIDI encoder, multi-scale temporal alignment, and three complementary conditioning strategies: early injection, Feature-wise Linear Modulation (FiLM), and cross-attention. We further show that providing the same piano roll only through classifier guidance, driven by an Automatic Drum Transcription (ADT) model on the audio-only score, yields no measurable gain: the symbolic prior is effective when it conditions the score network. To relax the requirement for ground-truth MIDI at inference, we further propose a hybrid reverse schedule that transcribes the diffusion state online with the same noise-aware ADT network and hands over from the audio-only score to MiDiff at a tunable switch time, cutting test FAD by 47% relative to the audio-only baseline without any symbolic input (switch time selected on the test set). We train our model on the StemGMD dataset using a non-additive degradation pipeline that simulates room reverberation with echo, electret capsule frequency response, and soft-clipping saturation with noise. MiDiff substantially outperforms the SGMSE baseline in terms of Fréchet Audio Distance (FAD) on both the validation and held-out test sets. Ablation studies demonstrate that combining all three conditioning strategies yields superior performance and that authentic MIDI velocity dynamics are critical for effective symbolic conditioning.
comment: 13 pages. Submitted to IEEE/ACM Transactions on Audio, Speech, and Language Processing. Audio demos and code: https://midiff-paper.github.io/midiff-project-page/
☆ DRC-TTS: A Dual-Resolution Codec-Based Architecture for Lexicon-Free Malay Speech Synthesis
Tianhui Su, Tien-Ping Tan
Modern discrete neural audio codecs facilitate speech synthesis by replacing continuous acoustic representations with low-frame-rate discrete token sequences. For Malay speech synthesis, character-level input reduces reliance on pronunciation lexicons. However, combining character-level inputs with low-frame-rate discrete codecs introduces a temporal alignment challenge. When predicted character durations are quantized into frame counts at 12.5 Hz, durations shorter than one codec frame may be assigned zero frames. Consequently, the corresponding character representations may be lost during length regulation, potentially leading to pronunciation omissions. This study proposes DRC-TTS, a dual-resolution codec-based architecture for lexicon-free Malay speech synthesis. The model expands character representations at a temporal resolution of 50 Hz and subsequently downsamples them through strided convolution to 12.5 Hz for discrete codec-token prediction. Objective evaluations show that the proposed model reduces the character error rate (CER) from 27.11% for the baseline to 21.86%, an absolute reduction of 5.25 percentage points. The proposed model also achieves a mean opinion score (MOS) of 4.30, compared with 4.12 for the baseline. These results suggest that the dual-resolution design may improve character-level alignment and perceived speech naturalness under the evaluated conditions.

☆ MixCards: Evaluating Structured Descriptions of Multi-Source Sound Scenes
Sripathi Sridhar, Yujin Kim, Giovana Morais, Liang-Yuan Wu, Mehmet Atilay Kucukoglu, Prem Seetharaman, Lloyd May, Mark Cartwright, Magdalena Fuentes
Audio captioning benchmarks typically evaluate a single unstructured free-text description of an audio scene, providing limited insight into how a model fails to understand polyphonic audio. A plausible caption may omit a source, or conflate multiple sources into one, or assign an attribute of one source to another, and conventional captioning evaluation cannot locate these errors. We introduce MixCardBench, a benchmark for structured captioning of polyphonic audio, which evaluates models in two stages: first, identifying and temporally localizing the sources in a scene, and second, generating a structured MixCard describing the semantic, temporal, and acoustic properties of each source. The benchmark contains 4884 ecologically plausible synthetic soundscapes with up to nine overlapping speech, music and sound effects sources built from high-quality recordings and source-level annotations, where each source has a reference MixCard. We evaluate six state-of-the-art large audio language models and find substantial limitations in current models, which struggle considerably with speech and sound effects timing and detection, with the strongest model reaching only around 60% mean card-field score. Performance varies significantly across attributes, exposing capability differences that are hidden by aggregate caption scores. We assess the quality and ecological validity of MixCardBench through human validation, distribution matching and a listening study, and show that human corrections have little effect on model rankings, and our synthesized soundscapes are closer to in-the-wild YouTube videos than source guided but otherwise random synthesis. The benchmark dataset and code are publicly available, and demo examples are at https://mixcards-anon.github.io/mixcards-demo/

☆ A Tutorial on Generative Models for Music Audio
Mateusz Modrzejewski, Joanna Kurkowska, Dorien Herremans
Music audio generation spans instrumental clips, full songs with vocals, edits of existing recordings, and systems that play alongside a musician in real time. This monograph explains the methods behind these systems for readers familiar with neural-network training who are new to music generation. It introduces neural audio codecs and autoencoders, autoregressive and masked token models, diffusion and flow matching, sampling acceleration, and preference optimization in a shared notation. Worked examples connect training objectives and sampling procedures to published systems. The application sections relate the musical requirements of instrumental generation, songs, editing, and live performance to model design. Comparison tables record representations, methods, inputs, tasks, and release information documented in papers and official sources. Symbolic composition, speech, and sound effects are included where they connect to music audio. We explain how to interpret automatic metrics and learned judges, design and report listening tests, and assess evidence about data provenance, memorization, attribution, and output detection. Selected legal decisions and disputes illustrate the implications for training and release. The reviewed systems combine established generative paradigms with new representations, planning stages, and post-training procedures. Differences in data, scale, and evaluation limit what cross-system comparisons can establish about the sources of reported gains.

☆ Partially Edited Audio: Generation, Defense, and Open Problems ICASSP 2027
Lin Zhang, You Zhang, Nicholas Evans, Xin Wang, David Harwath, Abhinav Dhall, Bowen Shi, Chengzhe Sun, Siwei Lyu, Sanjeev Khudanpur
Recent advances in generative audio models facilitate increasingly flexible and selective editing of linguistic content and paralinguistic, extralinguistic, and other attributes. This paradigm, named partially edited audio, differs from full audio generation as only portions of the real recording are edited. This technique can serve both beneficial and harmful applications. We therefore present a concise survey from both generation and defense perspectives, focusing on audio, as a contribution to the ICASSP 2027 special session entitled "Partially Edited Media: Perspectives from Synthesis and Defense." We first define partially edited audio and argue that what counts as ``fake'' or harmful is an application-dependent judgment, not a fixed property of the edit. We then survey audio editing by editing target, approaches, and evaluation, and then defense methods by detection, localization, diarization, and interpretability, summarizing representative benchmarks and toolkits. Finally, we discuss future directions and open problems.
comment: submitted to IEEE ICASSP 2027, 5 pages
☆ Beyond Answer Changes: Matched Same-Class Controls for Local Audio Evidence ICASSP 2027
Yunuo Wang, Maoyuan Chen, Yuanjin Huang, Xing Liu
For audio-language models, an answer change after a local sound-event edit can reflect a response to the event's class, sensitivity to waveform rewriting, or both. We compare matched same-class and different-class replacements of a queried event. Both use the same interval, level estimate, donor fitting, and crossfade, while the same-class replacement preserves the correct answer. Across 600 synthetic soundscapes and three models from two architecture families, different-class replacements produce 49.7 to 60.9 percentage points more answer changes than same-class replacements. Same-class accuracy remains within 5.2 percentage points of original accuracy. Among trials with correct original and same-class answers, soundscape-weighted selective accuracy for the inserted class is 73.7 to 81.9%, averaging eligible trials within each soundscape and then weighting eligible soundscapes equally. This protocol tests how model answers respond to local changes in event class.

☆ EmbeddingGemma 2: Unified and Efficient Multimodal Representations
Henrique Schechter Vera, Sahil Dua, Jovan Andonov, Sara Smoot, Sebastian Russo, Ivan Llanos, Max Matveev, Jae Hyeon Yoo, Kat Black, Shih-Cheng Huang, Josiah Aklilu, Maarten Grootendorst, Omar Sanseviero, Chandramouli Amarnath, Ian Ballantyne, Zhe Li, Daniel Salz, Ibrahim Alabdulmohsin, Ilya Philippov, Kristen Quan, Glenn Cameron, Edouard Yvinec, Luciano Martins, Doug Reid, Sindhu Raghuram Panyam, Weiyi Wang, Hengxuan Ying, Madhuri Shanbhogue, Tanmaya Dabral, Shanfeng Zhang, Juyeong Ji, Renjie Wu, Joe Zou, Xu Chen, Yunan Zhang, Yu-Hui Chen, Matthew Soulanille, Vinod Mamillapalli, Yi-Chun Kuo, Wai Hon Law, Matt Kreileder, Alice Zheng, Suril Shah, Mogan Shieh, Pooja Consul, Alberto Montes, Andreas Hess, Andres Sevilla, Babak Samari, Brendan McCloskey, Brian Potetz, Daniel Cer, Georgios Kathareios, Gustavo Hernández Ábrego, Hesen Zhang, Ji Ma, Jiaxing Wu, Keegan Mosley, Paul Suganthan, Rui Meng, Shen Gao, Shengcao Cao, Yi-Ting Chen, Yichang Chen, Zhongli Ding, Kendra Byrne, Cormac Brick, Olivier Lacombe, Qin Yin, Tris Warkentin, Armand Joulin, Tom Duerig, Mojtaba Seyedhosseini
We present EmbeddingGemma 2, an open multimodal embedding model which natively represents text, images, audio, video, and combinations thereof in a unified space. Our approach introduces improvements such as simplified per-layer embeddings and a multi-stage curriculum with modality and objective progression which ensure strong quality across unimodal, cross-modal, and mixed-modal evaluations. Notably, in comprehensive embedding benchmarks across all modalities, EmbeddingGemma 2 establishes a new Pareto frontier, outperforming both specialist models and models two to twelve times larger. Furthermore, our design offers flexibility for resource-constrained environments, supporting selective modality encoder loading, adjustable vision token budgets, truncatable embedding dimensions, and quantized weights. We present ablations analyzing key decisions and release EmbeddingGemma 2 to promote further research.

☆ Understanding Everyday Communication Patterns, Stress, and Productivity in Hybrid Work through Egocentric Wearable Audio Sensing
Tiantian Feng, Aditya Kommineni, Emily Zhou, Burcin Becerik-Gerber, Gale Lucas, Shawn C. Roll, Shrikanth Narayanan
The hybrid work trend in the post-COVID period has transformed how people communicate while at work. However, there is a lack of quantitative understanding of how home and office environments shape communicative behavior and affective well-being. To study this, as a part of a larger study of the role of work environment on stress, we designed an egocentric wearable audio sensing system that captured interpersonal communication across both working locations. The system extracts real-time acoustic features on a wearable audio sensor and performs offline foreground speaker diarization to derive speaking load and activeness features. To improve diarization performance under low-dimensional feature constraints, we apply a teacher-student knowledge distillation framework that transfers knowledge from large-scale speech foundation models into a compact ResNet-based model, achieving consistent improvements in diarization performance over the baseline across three public egocentric speech datasets. In a four-month longitudinal deployment with 16 participants, our system revealed location-dependent differences in work communication patterns. Moreover, the mixed linear model analyses showed that office-based speaking load was significantly associated with higher self-reported stress and lower self-reported productivity, while speaking activeness during home-based work amplified both productivity and affective load in this cohort.

☆ EEG-Based Decoding of Musical Mode and Melodic Direction Using Empirical Mode Decomposition
Sergio Guillén, Lorenzo J. Tardón, Ana M. Barbancho, Isabel Barbancho
Electroencephalography (EEG) has proven to be a powerful tool for decoding neural activity in real-life scenarios, including the perception and processing of emotions elicited by music. Among the various musical features that modulate these responses, musical mode and melodic direction (or contour) play a central role. This work proposes a novel EEG feature extraction framework based on Empirical Mode Decomposition (EMD) to decompose EEG signals recorded during active piano performance for the detection of these two musical features. Energy-based descriptors were computed from the first four Intrinsic Mode Functions (IMFs) obtained through EMD and used to train a Wide Neural Network classifier. The model performance was benchmarked against several standard classifiers commonly employed in EEG classification tasks. Two experimental scenarios were explored: intra-subject and intersubject. In the former case, the proposed framework achieved average accuracies of 84%, whereas in the inter-subject case, accuracies reached 81% on average using the first IMF, with AUC-ROC values of 0.9 on average in both cases. A frequency-domain analysis revealed a strong correspondence between the IMFs and conventional EEG sub-bands, except for certain specific frequency components that were not fully represented. Predominant activations were observed over the frontal, temporal, and parietooccipital regions, areas consistently associated with music processing. Furthermore, the proposed method demonstrated robustness to handedness, successfully classifying EEG data across participants regardless of their dominant hand. These findings highlight the potential of EMD-based feature extraction for identifying music-related neural patterns and contribute to advancing research in Music Information Retrieval (MIR), affective neuroscience, and the broader understanding of the neural encoding of musical structure.

☆ Design and Architecture of Airmod: An Active Noise Cancellation and Deep Learning System for Real-Time Respiratory Rate Estimation from Tracheal Sounds
Shang-Ran Huang, Fu-Shun Hsu, Ji-Chang Huang, Chuan Chen, Shou-Zen Fan, Chang-Fu Su, Eng-Che Huang, Yuan-Ren Cheng
Tracheal auscultation is recommended by clinical practice guidelines, and required by some U.S. state regulations, for monitoring ventilation during procedural sedation and monitored anesthesia care. However, continuous auscultation with a conventional stethoscope is impractical, susceptible to ambient noise, and difficult to interpret. We developed the Artificial Intelligence Respiratory MOnitoring Device (Airmod), an FDA-cleared software as a medical device (510(k) K242798) that continuously monitors tracheal sounds and estimates breath-to-breath respiratory rate in real time. In this paper, we describe its software architecture and key processing modules. Ambient noise is suppressed by active noise control, using a normalized least-mean-square adaptive filter with a dual-microphone electronic stethoscope. A multiclass convolutional bidirectional gated recurrent unit (CNN-BiGRU) model detects inhalations and exhalations in 15-s inference windows. It was trained on HF_Tracheal_V2, a new database of 373 continuous tracheal sound recordings (8,521 min; 107,644 labeled inhalations) from 369 subjects under sedation. To handle continuous acoustic streaming, Airmod runs inference on overlapping 15-s windows. It refines the detected inhalations by removing incomplete events, low-energy false positives, and double counts, concatenates them into a history list, and estimates respiratory rate from the mean period of the last three breaths. On the test set, at the default 2-s prediction interval with refinement enabled, inhalation detection achieved a sensitivity of 0.828, a positive predictive value of 0.832, and an F1-score of 0.830. Airmod also broadcasts the noise-cancelled tracheal sound and displays a real-time spectrogram to help clinicians recognize respiratory abnormalities.
☆ Perceptual Differences and Preferences in Speech Enhancement ICASSP 2027
Simon Dahl Jepsen, Jesper Rindom Jensen
Speech enhancement (SE) systems are commonly evaluated with objective metrics, with and without references, and with categorical subjective listening tests, all measuring speech quality and intelligibility. So far, it is unclear from such evaluations whether the processed speech is perceptually different or is preferred by everyday listeners. We investigate discrimination and preference as complementary dimensions of SE evaluation through crowdsourced triangle and pairwise preference tests across four SE systems, with comparisons to clean references. Results show that both listeners' ability to distinguish and whether they exhibit systematic preference vary across systems and substantially across acoustic conditions. Pairwise evaluations of objective metrics showed variable correlation with both discriminability and preference, motivating further studies into these novel aspects in speech enhancement evaluation.

☆ Physiology-Informed Audio Quality and Listening Effort Estimation
Niall McGuire, Dimitra Emmanouilidou
Audio systems aim to maximise the listener's perceived quality, traditionally evaluated through mean opinion scoring (MOS), a subjective process that is slow, costly, and collected only after playback. Machine learning now predicts MOS directly from the audio, but in generalising across participants it tends to discard the subject variance that defines individual perception. Neurophysiological measures may offer a complementary signal taken directly from the listener, objective, implicit, and continuous, though prior work has relied on laboratory-grade EEG and fNIRS. We ask how practical consumer-grade devices compare, and whether they might recover population-level audio-quality trends and, when calibrated per listener, track that listener's effort. Recording 32-channel laboratory EEG alongside wearable EEG, fNIRS, and eye tracking from thirty listeners, our results suggest commercial wearable and optical sensing can decode audio quality at statistically significant levels and recover listening effort per listener. These findings may point towards platforms tuned not only to perceived quality but to the effort a clip demands, read from the listener's own response as they listen.

☆ Expressive Guitar Synthesis via Controllable Latent Flow Matching ICASSP 2027
Hsueh-Wei Fu, Yen-Tung Yeh, Yi-Hsuan Yang
Realistic guitar synthesis requires both audio fidelity and interpretable control over how notes are performed. The input timed MIDI events decide what is played but not how, leaving the continuous within-note decisions of guitar performance--such as pitch inflection and per-string articulation--unspecified. A model that directly maps MIDI to audio must therefore realize the performance implicitly, and users are left with limited control over the synthesized performance. We therefore propose a two-stage guitar synthesis pipeline that predicts editable, per-string $f_0$ and amplitude trajectories from timed note events and note-level dynamics, and renders them into audio using latent flow matching. Experimental results show that the proposed system outperforms a matched single-stage counterpart and DDSP-Guitar in control fidelity and perceived quality, while keeping the controls editable. Sound examples can be found online.

☆ S3-S2ST: Semantically Supervised Streaming Speech-to-Speech Translation
Yuxiang Zhao, Zhiyun Fan, Yu Pu, Yanjie An, Yushen Chen, Wenrui Liang, Baiji Liu, Yunchong Xiao, Zhaoci Liu, Keqi Deng, Kai Yu, Zhifu Gao, Xiangang Li, Xie Chen
Streaming speech-to-speech translation requires timely decisions about when partial input is sufficient for accurate translation. We present S3-S2ST, a model that learns to translate and speak from semantically aligned streaming supervision. By converting utterance-level speech pairs into incremental training examples, we teach a learned policy when to commit translations. Its adjustable threshold controls the quality--latency tradeoff on a fixed 640\,ms input grid. S3-S2ST delivers competitive English--Chinese translation on FLEURS and leads the evaluated streaming systems in translation quality on the internal 9-pair test set. On RealSI, adapting the threshold to buffered speech further improves quality over a low fixed threshold with little change in first-audio latency. We plan to release the model and code.
☆ The Content Leash: Mitigating Degenerate Solutions in Invertible Speaker Anonymization
Nirjon Mobarak Talukder, Rafid Ahmed, Mohammad Ishrak Abedin, Abu Raihan Mostofa Kamal
Voice anonymization aims to protect a speaker's identity while preserving the linguistic content of speech, enabling voice data to be shared and processed with reduced privacy risk. This work focuses on reversible voice anonymization, where the original voice can be recovered by an authorized user rather than being permanently discarded. However, existing approaches can achieve apparent speaker anonymization by degrading the speech itself, while their effectiveness may also depend on the speaker-verification representation used during training. This creates a need for methods that protect speaker identity without sacrificing speech intelligibility and that remain effective against unseen speaker verifiers. We introduce content preserving training constraints to improve the privacy-utility trade-off by preventing anonymization from being achieved primarily through speech degradation. We further introduce a verifier-generalization strategy that incorporates a stronger speaker-verification representation during training, improving anonymization robustness beyond the verifier used in the original training setup. The resulting approach maintains intelligible speech, strengthens anonymization, and preserves reliable voice restoration, with evaluation on unseen speakers and held-out speaker verification models. On 38 unseen speakers, the approach raises the attacker's equal error rate from a measured floor of 2.8% to 26.3%, and to 27.9% against a held-out verifier, with 11.8% word error rate and 94.9% speaker similarity on key-based restoration. These improvements advance reversible voice anonymization toward practical privacy-preserving speech applications, where anonymized speech can be safely processed or shared while the original voice remains recoverable under authorized conditions.
☆ SMEBENCH: Benchmarking Neural Music Editing with Synthetized MIDI Edits
Matthieu Cervera, Francesco Paissan, Micael Antunes, Mirco Ravanelli, Ricard Marxer, Cem Subakan
Neural music editing requires a system to perform a requested change while preserving the musical content that should remain unchanged. Existing evaluations often lack a paired target edit, making these requirements difficult to measure separately. We introduce SMEBench, a large-scale benchmark of controlled music edits constructed by modifying symbolic MIDI performances and rendering matched source and target audio. Each example contains a source, an instruction, a paired target, edit metadata, and complementary descriptions. The benchmark covers twelve instrumentation, articulation, dynamics, and pitch operations and includes a balanced 3,600-example test set together with a smaller real-audio complement derived from multitrack recordings. The paired targets allow source preservation, target agreement, and textual compatibility to be evaluated independently. We use these references to diagnose common audio-editing metrics and benchmark six representative editing systems, showing that the metric used to rank a system can materially change the conclusion. The dataset is available at our repository.
☆ From Voiceprints to User Entities: Online Speaker-Memory Construction for Multi-User Spoken Agents
Yucong Zhang, Cancan Li, Bo Xiao, Ke Zeng, Ming Li
Personalized spoken agents must identify speakers before accessing user-specific memory, yet memory benchmarks typically assume correctly attributed histories. We argue that voiceprints are observations of identity, not identities themselves, and formulate online speaker-memory construction to maintain persistent user entities as acoustic evidence evolves. We introduce EvoSpeakerMem, a training-free layer for causal speaker routing, selective acoustic-state updates, and identity-partitioned memory writes and retrieval through a replaceable text-memory backend. We also construct LoCoMo-ID, a spoken-memory benchmark with hidden speaker identities, speaker-sensitive queries, simulated recording-condition shifts, and four-speaker identity-confusion tests. On longitudinal SMIIP-TV, genuine-probe rejection under a frozen near-enrollment threshold rises from 29.8% to 55.6% over approximately one year. On LoCoMo-ID speaker-sensitive queries, gated updating improves identity-gated QA over fixed representations by 3.86 and 11.62 percentage points under clean and shifted conditions, respectively, with no wrong-user authorizations. The advantage persists in the four-speaker test. Yet reducing fragmentation and improving QA can coexist with incorrect cross-user links, revealing a fragmentation--contamination trade-off that QA alone cannot capture.

☆ Tap2Listen: Instant Target Switching for Streaming Audio-Visual Speaker Extraction NeurIPS 2026
Hansol Park, Minkyung Song, Zinu Kim, Yujun Lee, Hoseong Ahn, Hyunjin Choi, Kyuhong Shim
Streaming audio-visual target speaker extraction (AV-TSE) uses a target speaker's face to extract the speaker's speech from an input audio mixture in real time. However, existing systems fix the target speaker for an entire clip, while conversation demands frequent and immediate target switches. To address this problem, we propose Tap2Listen, a streaming AV-TSE model designed for instant response to target switches. The model separates computation by modality: the target-agnostic audio encoder processes only the mixture, while the target-specific visual cues of the selected face condition only the decoder. A switch requires only a 0.12ms re-projection and takes effect immediately. We also design component-wise losses: a prediction loss for the encoder and a supervised extraction loss for the decoder. For evaluation, we measure how quickly output quality recovers after a switch. On the standard LRS3-2mix test set, Tap2Listen improves SI-SNRi from 8.85 to 9.68 dB at a comparable parameter count. After a switch to a known face, the model produces full-quality output from the first frame, whereas the baseline needs about 1 second to recover. Finally, we show that the proposed streaming AV-TSE model runs in real time on a single CPU core.

☆ AudioRSI: Recursively Self-Improving Audio Reasoners
Jiajun Fan, Roger Ren, Jingyuan Li, Rahul Pandey, Prashanth Gurunath Shivakumar, Ankur Gandhe, Yile Gu, Ge Liu, Ivan Bulyko
Reinforcement learning has made Audio Large Language Models (Audio LLMs) better reasoners, but the reward that drives it still comes from outside the model: a final-answer check, a hand-crafted process score, or an external LLM judge that stays fixed while the policy improves. We show that an Audio LLM can supply this reward itself, and can do so recursively: each improved model becomes the critic that trains its successor, so the training signal improves along with the model. We introduce AudioRSI (Recursively Self-Improving Audio Reasoners), a reinforcement learning framework in which a single model plays two roles: as an actor it generates reasoning paths, and as a critic it compares them pairwise, turning its own judgments into a process-level reward. The critic is periodically replaced by the current policy, which closes the recursive loop. Because the critic hears the same recording as the actor, it can reject reasoning that cites acoustic evidence the audio does not contain, rather than reward reasoning that merely sounds plausible. The recursion is what sustains progress: under a frozen external judge, out-of-distribution accuracy plateaus during training, while a critic refreshed from the improving policy keeps it rising. Across four out-of-distribution benchmarks, all disjoint from the AVQA training distribution, AudioRSI outperforms strong baselines including Audio Flamingo 3 and Gemini 2.5 Pro on MMAU test-mini, ranks first on MMSU, achieves a clear lead on the challenging Multi-Audio split of MMAU-Pro, and leads the 7B open-source tier on MMAR among methods without external reward models. With no reward specifying how to reason, AudioRSI also develops structured reasoning behaviors (logical reasoning, perception-aware analysis, and reduced hallucination), corroborated by an external LLM-as-Judge evaluation and a keyword-based behavior analysis.

☆ TAC2: Timestamped Audio Captioning as composable functions
Swapnil Bhosale, Prem Seetharaman, Ke Chen, Haonan Chen, Justin Salamon, Zeyu Jin
Real-world audio applications require precise, queryable representations grounded in physical time. Yet modern Large Audio-Language Models (LALMs) increasingly favor conversational generation, producing free-form descriptions that conflate acoustic perception with higher-level reasoning and lack precise temporal grounding. We introduce TAC2, a foundation model that casts timestamped audio captioning as composable functions to construct granular, speaker-attributed acoustic timelines directly from in-the-wild audio. To avoid prohibitively expensive manual annotation, we programmatically fuse complementary predictions from specialized weak teachers through time-registered IoU matching. We model the resulting multi-granularity schema of timestamped events, speaker turns, and fine-grained speech attributes using an Instruction-Input-Output (IIO) completion format, in which each task is a function of the audio, an instruction, and an optional input. A single call decodes the full description autonomously, while composing calls lets earlier outputs or external priors, such as a reference transcript, condition later ones. We further extend TAC2 with expressive speech attributes to obtain TAC2-S, using parameter-efficient specialists to elicit latent paralinguistic capabilities from the pre-trained backbone and distill them into a unified model. We validate the resulting representation in two complementary settings. Paired with frozen text-only LLMs, it yields strong spoken audio understanding across diverse reasoning backends, demonstrating the utility of decoupling fine-grained acoustic perception from downstream reasoning. Used as paired supervision for text-to-audio generation, it supports semantically and temporally grounded reconstruction, together with explicit zero-shot control over event timing, speaker attributes, and word-level emphasis.

☆ Beyond Utterance-Level Speaker Similarity: Perception-Aligned Segmental Evaluation of Accent in Speech Generation
Jinzuomu Zhong, Alice Ross, Catherine Lai, Korin Richmond
Utterance-level similarity ratings do not reveal where perceived accent differences occur in generated speech. We introduce a segmental evaluation protocol combining speaker and accent similarity ratings with subword annotations of perceived accent differences provided by listeners from target accent regions. Using newly collected recordings, 47 retained listeners evaluate 200 content-matched reference--candidate pairs spanning four Scottish and Australian voices, two zero-shot TTS systems, and an articulation-based voice conversion system. Subword annotations locate salient pronunciation differences and sometimes yield different system rankings from similarity ratings. Speaker and accent ratings remain strongly associated ($ρ= 0.71$), highlighting the value of examining local perceptual evidence beyond these scores. Evaluation of seven objective distances reveals weak correspondence with subword selections, with correlations reaching at most $ρ= 0.22$. We release code, data, and an interactive demo to support the development of perceptually grounded segmental accent evaluation.
☆ Universal Short-Time Fourier Transform: Data-Adaptive Window-Length Selection for Time-Frequency Analysis
Manan Mittal, Kanad Sarkar, Ryan M. Corey, John R. Buck, Andrew C. Singer
The short-time Fourier transform (STFT) characterizes the local frequency content of time-varying signals by evaluating the discrete Fourier transform over a sliding analysis window. The STFT is governed by a fundamental resolution trade-off: a short window localizes rapid transients in time at the cost of frequency resolution, whereas a long window resolves closely spaced harmonics at the expense of temporal resolution. The Universal Short-Time Fourier Transform (U-STFT) resolves this trade-off sequentially by modeling the analysis window duration as a data-adaptive state variable that indexes the number of hops included in the current observation interval. At each frame, a bank of candidate window durations is scored using normalized order-three Rényi entropy to quantify joint time-frequency concentration. A window length trellis aggregates the resulting $\mathcal{O}(3^M)$ candidate window schedules with linear complexity per frame, guaranteeing a cumulative mix-loss regret bound of $\mathcal{O}((k+1)\log M)$ relative to any hindsight window schedule with $k$ resolution changes over $M$ frames. By linearity of the Fourier transform, posterior expectation across the candidate bank yields a single spectrum equivalent to an STFT evaluated with a data-adaptive effective window, while an envelope-normalized synthesis stream guarantees exact overlap-add reconstruction. Evaluations on synthetic and marine bioacoustic signals demonstrate adaptive resolution tracking, enhanced spectral concentration, and exact time-domain invertibility.
comment: 12 pages; 7 figures; SANE 2026, ASA 2026
♻ ☆ Correspondence Is Not Transfer: A Pairing-Controlled Study of Clinical Audio-Metadata Alignment
Liu He, Xi Wang, Jiahong Yuan, Yuanchao Li
Clinical audio models are often trained by aligning recordings with participant metadata or text derived from it. This metadata is rarely a clean disease signal, since a single profile also contains symptoms, age, sex, missing responses, and recruitment information. We examine what alignment adds to frozen audio features by varying only the audio-meta data pairing. We keep the audio backbones fixed and train only a projector under correct pairing and three shuffled conditions that progressively preserve the disease label and recorded sex. We then evaluate each projector on profile retrieval, attribute probing, and disease classification on covariate-matched test sets. On UKCOVID, correct pairing clearly improves retrieval and makes sex easier to decode, confirming that the pairing manipulation works. Most of the sex-probe gap disappears when the control also preserves recorded sex, while a small retrieval gap remains. Matched disease AUROC differences are small, and every interval includes zero, so modest benefits or harms are not ruled out. The same pattern appears when we rerun the frozen pipeline on CODA TB, Cambridge COVID-19 Sounds, and Coswara, where retrieval and sex-probe contrasts are consistently positive but disease contrasts are not. We find no consistent evidence that better profile correspondence translates into better disease prediction and suggest reporting these outcomes separately.
♻ ☆ A Benchmark for Controllable Speaking-Style Captioning in Audio-Language Models ACL 2026
Shreeram Suresh Chandra, Ashwyn Sharma, Liang Lu, Xiutian Zhao, Leda Sari, Björn Schuller, Berrak Sisman
Speaking-style captioning (SSC) aims to generate natural language descriptions of how speech is delivered, capturing paralinguistic attributes such as vocal timbre, prosody, and expressivity. Many downstream applications, including conversational AI agents, controllable speech generation, and large-scale audio annotation, require dimension-specific style captions that describe targeted aspects of speech (e.g., speaker traits, emotion, or delivery style), rather than a single undifferentiated description. However, existing work lacks a unified formulation for controllable speaking-style captioning. We address this gap by formulating SSC as an instruction-following audio-language task, where explicit instructions specify the speaking-style dimensions to be described. We introduce StyleInstructCaps, the first standardized benchmark for controllable speaking-style captioning in audio-language models. StyleInstructCaps provides a dataset and evaluation framework that measures metadata groundedness, hallucination, instruction-following ability, generalization to unseen instructions and audio datasets, and speaker-style consistency. Across nine state-of-the-art audio-language models, we find that strong instruction-following ability does not necessarily imply grounded speaking-style understanding, and that SSC-specific instruction-diverse training substantially improves groundedness, controllability, and speaker consistency.
comment: Accepted at AACL 2026. Code, data, and benchmark are available at https://styleinstructcaps.github.io
♻ ☆ Streaming Generation for Music Accompaniment
Yusong Wu, Mason Wang, Heidi Lei, Stephen Brade, Lancelot Blanchard, Shih-Lun Wu, Aaron Courville, Anna Huang
Music generation models can produce high-fidelity coherent accompaniment given complete audio input, but are limited to editing and loop-based workflows. We study real-time audio-to-audio accompaniment: as a model hears an input audio stream (e.g., a singer singing), it has to also simultaneously generate in real-time a coherent accompanying stream (e.g., a guitar accompaniment). In this work, we propose a model design considering inevitable system delays in practical deployment with two design variables: future visibility $t_f$, the offset between the output playback time and the latest input time used for conditioning, and output chunk duration $k$, the number of frames emitted per call. We train Transformer decoders across a grid of $(t_f,k)$ and show two consistent trade-offs: increasing effective $t_f$ improves coherence by reducing the recency gap, but requires faster inference to stay within the latency budget; increasing $k$ improves throughput but results in degraded accompaniment due to a reduced update rate. Finally, we observe that naive maximum-likelihood streaming training is insufficient for coherent accompaniment where future context is not available, motivating advanced anticipatory and agentic objectives for live jamming.

♻ ☆ Integrated Spoofing-Robust Automatic Speaker Verification via a Three-Class Formulation and LLR
Kai Tan, Lin Zhang, Ruiteng Zhang, Johan Rohdin, Leibny Paola García-Perera, Zexin Cai, Sanjeev Khudanpur, Matthew Wiesner, Nicholas Andrews
Spoofing-robust automatic speaker verification (SASV) aims to integrate automatic speaker verification (ASV) and countermeasure (CM). A popular solution is fusion of independent ASV and CM scores. To better modeling SASV, some frameworks integrate ASV and CM within a single network. However, these solutions are typically bi-encoder based, offer limited interpretability, and cannot be readily adapted to new evaluation parameters without retraining. Based on this, we propose a unified end-to-end framework via a three-class formulation that enables log-likelihood ratio (LLR) inference from class logits for a more interpretable decision pipeline. Experiments show comparable performance to existing methods on ASVSpoof5 and better results on SpoofCeleb. The visualization and analysis also prove that the three-class reformulation provides more interpretability.

♻ ☆ Spatio-Temporal Audio Language Modeling for Dynamic Sound Sources EMNLP 2026
Oh Hyun-Bin, Kazuki Shimada, Yuhta Takida, Kim Sung-Bin, Toshimitsu Uesaka, Takashi Shibuya, Kyeongyoon Lee, Tae-Hyun Oh, Yuki Mitsufuji
Sound events have semantic identities, locations, and trajectories, yet existing audio-language models typically encode clips as global event content. Conversely, sound event localization models track source directions over time but offer limited semantic coverage for language reasoning. To bridge this gap, we introduce ST-AudioQA, a spatio-temporal audio QA dataset and benchmark built from first-order ambisonic (FOA) renderings of static and moving sound sources. Each scene provides source identity, activity, direction, distance, and motion metadata, enabling dense trajectory supervision and QA about what is sounding, where it is, how it moves, and how sources relate. We further introduce ST-Audio Encoder, which jointly learns event semantics and time-resolved source trajectories, and ST-AudioLM, which exposes these audio tokens to an LLM for spatio-temporal audio QA. Experiments show that this representation improves the balance between semantic preservation and localization and yields stronger reasoning than static spatial and localization-oriented baselines. Beyond the controlled benchmark, ST-AudioLM shows zero-shot transfer to real recordings, with further gains after light adaptation. Project page: https://st-audiolm.github.io/.

♻ ☆ The SonicAGI System for the REAL-TSE Challenge
Kai Li, Wendi Sang, Jintao Cheng, Xiaolin Hu
Real-world target speaker extraction (TSE) remains challenging because target speech, interference, and enrollment are recorded under mismatched acoustic conditions with reverberation, noise, and irregular conversational overlap. This paper describes the SonicAGI submission to the REAL-TSE Challenge (IEEE SLT 2026). We take a data-centric approach that combines fully simulated mixtures from clean speech with real meeting overlaps, and use a frozen offline enhancer to provide a denoised mirror of real targets for auxiliary supervision. For the online track, we introduce SwiftNet-Lookahead, which inserts a single bounded-lookahead module before a strictly causal iterative separator and keeps the total system latency at 96 ms. For the offline track, we use a frame-level enrollment cross-attention USEF-TFGridNet with a magnitude-domain fusion stage designed to balance perceptual quality and speaker fidelity. In the final verified Phase-1 ranking, SwiftNet-Lookahead ranks third in Track 1 and USEF-TFGridNet ranks fifth in Track 2, both exceeding the challenge baselines. These results suggest that real-data-oriented training and track-specific modeling are effective for conversational TSE.
♻ ☆ CrossEdit: Cross-Modal Training Enables Rich Audio-Visual Editing
William Chen, Prem Seetharaman, Ke Chen, Oriol Nieto, Kevin Duarte, Siddharth Srinivasan Iyer, Mamshad Nayeem Rizve, Zhiwen Cao, Shinji Watanabe, Yuanjun Xiong, Jianming Zhang, Zeyu Jin, Justin Salamon
Multimedia editing requires generative models to interpret complex, compositional instructions and modify only the desired elements across modalities, a capability largely beyond existing systems. Current approaches are typically limited to simple, single-attribute edits within one modality, since diverse, high-quality editing pairs are hard to obtain, especially for cross-modal tasks where aligned audiovisual (AV) data is scarce. We present CrossEdit, a unified omni-modal editing model for images, audio, and video that performs AV movie scene edits zero-shot through cross-modal transfer. Our key observation is that complex instruction-following, once learned in any modality, generalizes to others. We exploit the additive nature of acoustic signals to procedurally generate large-scale audio editing pairs with compositional instructions, and show that fine-tuning on this synthetic data and self-supervised AV masked reconstruction, alongside a targeted set of curated cross-modal tasks, induces instruction-following that transfers zero-shot to unseen modality and instruction combinations. To evaluate this capability, we release CrossEditBench, a human-annotated benchmark of AV edits on movie scenes, and propose AV-FES, a metric that jointly scores instruction following and consistency. We show that our proposed techniques improve performance on zero-shot AV movie scene editing, while maintaining or improving performance on lip-synced speech editing and standard image, video, and audio editing benchmarks. Demos are available at https://wanchichen.github.io/crossedit/.

♻ ☆ LibriVAD: A Scalable Open Dataset with Deep Learning Benchmarks for Robust Voice Activity Detection
Ioannis Stylianou, Achintya kr. Sarkar, Nauman Dawalatabad, James Glass, Zheng-Hua Tan
Robust Voice Activity Detection (VAD) remains a challenging task, especially under noisy, diverse, and unseen acoustic conditions. Beyond algorithmic development, a key limitation in advancing VAD research is the lack of large-scale, systematically controlled, and publicly available datasets. To address this, we introduce \textbf{LibriVAD} -- a scalable open-source dataset derived from LibriSpeech and augmented with diverse real-world and synthetic noise sources. LibriVAD enables systematic control over speech-to-noise ratio, silence-to-speech ratio (SSR), and noise diversity, and is released in three sizes (15 GB, 150 GB, and 1.5 TB) with two variants (LibriVAD-NonConcat and LibriVAD-Concat) to support different experimental setups. We benchmark multiple feature-model combinations, including waveform, Mel-Frequency Cepstral Coefficients (MFCC), and Gammatone filter bank cepstral coefficients, and introduce the Vision Transformer (ViT) architecture for VAD. Our experiments show that ViT with MFCC features consistently outperforms established VAD models such as boosted deep neural network and convolutional long short-term memory deep neural network across seen, unseen, and out-of-distribution (OOD) conditions, including evaluation on the real-world VOiCES dataset. We further analyze the impact of dataset size and SSR on model generalization. Experimental results show that scaling the dataset size from small-scale to medium- or large-scale noticeably and consistently improves VAD performance under OOD conditions, while appropriately balancing SSR enhances OOD performance in the small-scale setting. All datasets, trained models, and code are publicly available to foster reproducibility and accelerate progress in VAD research.

☆ Partially Edited Audio: Generation, Defense, and Open Problems ICASSP 2027
Lin Zhang, You Zhang, Nicholas Evans, Xin Wang, David Harwath, Abhinav Dhall, Bowen Shi, Chengzhe Sun, Siwei Lyu, Sanjeev Khudanpur
Recent advances in generative audio models facilitate increasingly flexible and selective editing of linguistic content and paralinguistic, extralinguistic, and other attributes. This paradigm, named partially edited audio, differs from full audio generation as only portions of the real recording are edited. This technique can serve both beneficial and harmful applications. We therefore present a concise survey from both generation and defense perspectives, focusing on audio, as a contribution to the ICASSP 2027 special session entitled "Partially Edited Media: Perspectives from Synthesis and Defense." We first define partially edited audio and argue that what counts as ``fake'' or harmful is an application-dependent judgment, not a fixed property of the edit. We then survey audio editing by editing target, approaches, and evaluation, and then defense methods by detection, localization, diarization, and interpretability, summarizing representative benchmarks and toolkits. Finally, we discuss future directions and open problems.

☆ StreamSE: Neural Audio Codec-based Streaming Speech Enhancement for On-device Inference NeurIPS 2026
Hyunjin Choi, Zinu Kim, Junwon Moon, Jeongyun Chae, Seungbeom Kim, Kyuhong Shim
Recent generative speech enhancement (SE) models achieve high perceptual quality, but their non-causal processing and expensive computation make them difficult to use for streaming, on-device inference. We propose StreamSE, a 20M-parameter streaming SE model that operates in the latent space of a frozen pretrained neural audio codec. At each frame, StreamSE directly regresses a clean continuous latent from the noisy continuous latent while conditioning on its own predictions from previous frames. Enhancement therefore requires a single forward pass per frame and no iterative sampling or look-ahead. We further truncate the codec's residual vector quantizer (RVQ) to its coarse levels, halving the number of tokens per frame while improving robustness to reverberation. StreamSE is the only streaming generative model in our comparison, yet it matches or exceeds the perceptual quality of the offline generative baselines. Furthermore, the complete StreamSE pipeline runs in real time on a single smartphone CPU core. Our results show that continuous latent regression provides a practical route to generative SE under fully causal, on-device streaming constraints.

☆ Developing a Speech Language Model for Basque
Andoni Sudupe, Inma Hernaez, Ander Arriandiaga, Christoforos Souganidis, Ibon Saratxaga, Eva Navas
Although the recent development of LLMs has paved the way for multi-modal interaction, minority languages face difficulties keeping pace. This work presents the first open Speech Language Model for Basque, designed for low-latency, end-to-end spoken interaction. Based on the LLaMA-Omni architecture, the system integrates a Latxa model as its backbone, transferring its Basque capabilities to the spoken modality by fine-tuning several modules. To address data scarcity, the English VoiceAssistant-400K corpus was translated into Basque, and the audio was synthesized using a Basque TTS. Evaluation results confirm the system's viability, achieving 3.86/5 in content quality, a 9.94% WER for spoken intelligibility, and a 3.07 UTMOS for audio quality. This work demonstrates that advanced spoken interaction systems can be developed using modular architectures and synthetic data even in low-resource languages.

☆ Perceptual Differences and Preferences in Speech Enhancement ICASSP 2027
Simon Dahl Jepsen, Jesper Rindom Jensen
Speech enhancement (SE) systems are commonly evaluated with objective metrics, with and without references, and with categorical subjective listening tests, all measuring speech quality and intelligibility. So far, it is unclear from such evaluations whether the processed speech is perceptually different or is preferred by everyday listeners. We investigate discrimination and preference as complementary dimensions of SE evaluation through crowdsourced triangle and pairwise preference tests across four SE systems, with comparisons to clean references. Results show that both listeners' ability to distinguish and whether they exhibit systematic preference vary across systems and substantially across acoustic conditions. Pairwise evaluations of objective metrics showed variable correlation with both discriminability and preference, motivating further studies into these novel aspects in speech enhancement evaluation.

☆ A Lightweight Dual-Branch Visual Front-End for Efficient Audio-Visual Target Speaker Extraction
Zhan Jin, Peijun Yang, Juan Liu, Ming Li
Audio-Visual Target Speaker Extraction (AVTSE) uses face-related visual cues to extract a target speaker from a speech mixture. In many AVTSE systems, visual features are obtained from convolutional image encoders, and their computation may become a non-negligible part of the overall system when lightweight separation backbones are used. This work proposes a dual-branch visual front-end that reorganizes visual information according to its spatial characteristics. A compact lip region of interest is used to model local articulation cues through convolutional processing, while facial landmark coordinates are used to represent global geometric motion with a lightweight temporal convolutional network. The two representations are integrated into IIANet and SpatialNet with limited fusion overhead. Experiments on LRS3-2mix under a unified reduced training protocol show that the proposed method achieves a performance-computation trade-off close to the lightweight image-based baseline. Compared with the ResNet18-based visual encoder, it reduces the module-level visual encoding computation by more than 90% across both evaluated separation backbones, with a moderate performance gap. This comparison excludes face detection and landmark estimation and therefore applies to systems where landmark coordinates are already available from preprocessing. Demos are available at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/Lightweight-Visual-Frontend-E46E.
☆ SMEBENCH: Benchmarking Neural Music Editing with Synthetized MIDI Edits
Matthieu Cervera, Francesco Paissan, Micael Antunes, Mirco Ravanelli, Ricard Marxer, Cem Subakan
Neural music editing requires a system to perform a requested change while preserving the musical content that should remain unchanged. Existing evaluations often lack a paired target edit, making these requirements difficult to measure separately. We introduce SMEBench, a large-scale benchmark of controlled music edits constructed by modifying symbolic MIDI performances and rendering matched source and target audio. Each example contains a source, an instruction, a paired target, edit metadata, and complementary descriptions. The benchmark covers twelve instrumentation, articulation, dynamics, and pitch operations and includes a balanced 3,600-example test set together with a smaller real-audio complement derived from multitrack recordings. The paired targets allow source preservation, target agreement, and textual compatibility to be evaluated independently. We use these references to diagnose common audio-editing metrics and benchmark six representative editing systems, showing that the metric used to rank a system can materially change the conclusion. The dataset is available at our repository.
☆ From Voiceprints to User Entities: Online Speaker-Memory Construction for Multi-User Spoken Agents
Yucong Zhang, Cancan Li, Bo Xiao, Ke Zeng, Ming Li
Personalized spoken agents must identify speakers before accessing user-specific memory, yet memory benchmarks typically assume correctly attributed histories. We argue that voiceprints are observations of identity, not identities themselves, and formulate online speaker-memory construction to maintain persistent user entities as acoustic evidence evolves. We introduce EvoSpeakerMem, a training-free layer for causal speaker routing, selective acoustic-state updates, and identity-partitioned memory writes and retrieval through a replaceable text-memory backend. We also construct LoCoMo-ID, a spoken-memory benchmark with hidden speaker identities, speaker-sensitive queries, simulated recording-condition shifts, and four-speaker identity-confusion tests. On longitudinal SMIIP-TV, genuine-probe rejection under a frozen near-enrollment threshold rises from 29.8% to 55.6% over approximately one year. On LoCoMo-ID speaker-sensitive queries, gated updating improves identity-gated QA over fixed representations by 3.86 and 11.62 percentage points under clean and shifted conditions, respectively, with no wrong-user authorizations. The advantage persists in the four-speaker test. Yet reducing fragmentation and improving QA can coexist with incorrect cross-user links, revealing a fragmentation--contamination trade-off that QA alone cannot capture.

☆ Improving the Dependency on Fine-Tuning Data in Transfer Learning for Speech Emotion Recognition
Ricardo García, Rodrigo Mahu, Carlos Busso, Néstor Becerra Yoma
Compensating for train-test mismatches in acoustic environments is important for deployable speech solutions. This paper proposes to reduce the amount of fine-tuning data needed in transfer learning to mitigate the train-test mismatch by using a compensation mechanism based on the feature maximum likelihood linear regression (fMLLR) algorithm. Our scheme incorporates an autoencoder to reduce the number of trainable parameters. Operating on the encoder latent space, our compensation strategy employs an affine linear transform that accounts for rotations and shifts in the feature space. We evaluate the proposed solution in a speech emotion recognition (SER) task within a realistic human-robot interaction scenario. The results show that the proposed architecture outperforms the original scheme without the compensation strategy. We observe a performance gain in the mean concordance correlation coefficient (CCC) of 16.8% using 12.9% of the training set, and 14.4% using 50% of the training set.

☆ ODAQ-Collection: Expanding the Open Dataset of Audio Quality with a Focus on Spatial Distortions
Chih-Wei Wu, Matteo Torcoli, Mhd Modar Halimeh, Pablo M. Delgado, Sascha Dick, Christoph Thompson, Phillip A. Williams, Emanuël A. P. Habets
The Open Dataset of Audio Quality (ODAQ) is an expanding resource that addresses the scarcity of openly available data in audio quality assessment research. While previous contributions focused mainly on timbral distortions, with spatial processing limited to basic mid-side and left-right stereo conditions, we present a new contribution featuring high-quality music and speech recordings with diverse stereo images, controlled spatial distortions, and subjective listening test results from trained listeners in a laboratory setting. With 148 pairs of stereo audio samples processed by three different method classes, two applying controlled binaural cue distortions and one applying dialogue enhancement, this addition expands the collection to 688 pairs of processed and unprocessed audio signals spanning 17 processing method classes, along with 18,984 raw subjective ratings from listeners. All associated data and code are released as open resources to facilitate future expansions and research on objective audio quality metrics.

☆ Beyond Utterance-Level Speaker Similarity: Perception-Aligned Segmental Evaluation of Accent in Speech Generation
Jinzuomu Zhong, Alice Ross, Catherine Lai, Korin Richmond
Utterance-level similarity ratings do not reveal where perceived accent differences occur in generated speech. We introduce a segmental evaluation protocol combining speaker and accent similarity ratings with subword annotations of perceived accent differences provided by listeners from target accent regions. Using newly collected recordings, 47 retained listeners evaluate 200 content-matched reference--candidate pairs spanning four Scottish and Australian voices, two zero-shot TTS systems, and an articulation-based voice conversion system. Subword annotations locate salient pronunciation differences and sometimes yield different system rankings from similarity ratings. Speaker and accent ratings remain strongly associated ($ρ= 0.71$), highlighting the value of examining local perceptual evidence beyond these scores. Evaluation of seven objective distances reveals weak correspondence with subword selections, with correlations reaching at most $ρ= 0.22$. We release code, data, and an interactive demo to support the development of perceptually grounded segmental accent evaluation.
☆ Universal Short-Time Fourier Transform: Data-Adaptive Window-Length Selection for Time-Frequency Analysis
Manan Mittal, Kanad Sarkar, Ryan M. Corey, John R. Buck, Andrew C. Singer
The short-time Fourier transform (STFT) characterizes the local frequency content of time-varying signals by evaluating the discrete Fourier transform over a sliding analysis window. The STFT is governed by a fundamental resolution trade-off: a short window localizes rapid transients in time at the cost of frequency resolution, whereas a long window resolves closely spaced harmonics at the expense of temporal resolution. The Universal Short-Time Fourier Transform (U-STFT) resolves this trade-off sequentially by modeling the analysis window duration as a data-adaptive state variable that indexes the number of hops included in the current observation interval. At each frame, a bank of candidate window durations is scored using normalized order-three Rényi entropy to quantify joint time-frequency concentration. A window length trellis aggregates the resulting $\mathcal{O}(3^M)$ candidate window schedules with linear complexity per frame, guaranteeing a cumulative mix-loss regret bound of $\mathcal{O}((k+1)\log M)$ relative to any hindsight window schedule with $k$ resolution changes over $M$ frames. By linearity of the Fourier transform, posterior expectation across the candidate bank yields a single spectrum equivalent to an STFT evaluated with a data-adaptive effective window, while an envelope-normalized synthesis stream guarantees exact overlap-add reconstruction. Evaluations on synthetic and marine bioacoustic signals demonstrate adaptive resolution tracking, enhanced spectral concentration, and exact time-domain invertibility.
comment: 12 pages; 7 figures; SANE 2026, ASA 2026
♻ ☆ Correspondence Is Not Transfer: A Pairing-Controlled Study of Clinical Audio-Metadata Alignment
Liu He, Xi Wang, Jiahong Yuan, Yuanchao Li
Clinical audio models are often trained by aligning recordings with participant metadata or text derived from it. This metadata is rarely a clean disease signal, since a single profile also contains symptoms, age, sex, missing responses, and recruitment information. We examine what alignment adds to frozen audio features by varying only the audio-meta data pairing. We keep the audio backbones fixed and train only a projector under correct pairing and three shuffled conditions that progressively preserve the disease label and recorded sex. We then evaluate each projector on profile retrieval, attribute probing, and disease classification on covariate-matched test sets. On UKCOVID, correct pairing clearly improves retrieval and makes sex easier to decode, confirming that the pairing manipulation works. Most of the sex-probe gap disappears when the control also preserves recorded sex, while a small retrieval gap remains. Matched disease AUROC differences are small, and every interval includes zero, so modest benefits or harms are not ruled out. The same pattern appears when we rerun the frozen pipeline on CODA TB, Cambridge COVID-19 Sounds, and Coswara, where retrieval and sex-probe contrasts are consistently positive but disease contrasts are not. We find no consistent evidence that better profile correspondence translates into better disease prediction and suggest reporting these outcomes separately.
♻ ☆ A Benchmark for Controllable Speaking-Style Captioning in Audio-Language Models ACL 2026
Shreeram Suresh Chandra, Ashwyn Sharma, Liang Lu, Xiutian Zhao, Leda Sari, Björn Schuller, Berrak Sisman
Speaking-style captioning (SSC) aims to generate natural language descriptions of how speech is delivered, capturing paralinguistic attributes such as vocal timbre, prosody, and expressivity. Many downstream applications, including conversational AI agents, controllable speech generation, and large-scale audio annotation, require dimension-specific style captions that describe targeted aspects of speech (e.g., speaker traits, emotion, or delivery style), rather than a single undifferentiated description. However, existing work lacks a unified formulation for controllable speaking-style captioning. We address this gap by formulating SSC as an instruction-following audio-language task, where explicit instructions specify the speaking-style dimensions to be described. We introduce StyleInstructCaps, the first standardized benchmark for controllable speaking-style captioning in audio-language models. StyleInstructCaps provides a dataset and evaluation framework that measures metadata groundedness, hallucination, instruction-following ability, generalization to unseen instructions and audio datasets, and speaker-style consistency. Across nine state-of-the-art audio-language models, we find that strong instruction-following ability does not necessarily imply grounded speaking-style understanding, and that SSC-specific instruction-diverse training substantially improves groundedness, controllability, and speaker consistency.
comment: Accepted at AACL 2026. Code, data, and benchmark are available at https://styleinstructcaps.github.io
♻ ☆ Integrated Spoofing-Robust Automatic Speaker Verification via a Three-Class Formulation and LLR
Kai Tan, Lin Zhang, Ruiteng Zhang, Johan Rohdin, Leibny Paola García-Perera, Zexin Cai, Sanjeev Khudanpur, Matthew Wiesner, Nicholas Andrews
Spoofing-robust automatic speaker verification (SASV) aims to integrate automatic speaker verification (ASV) and countermeasure (CM). A popular solution is fusion of independent ASV and CM scores. To better modeling SASV, some frameworks integrate ASV and CM within a single network. However, these solutions are typically bi-encoder based, offer limited interpretability, and cannot be readily adapted to new evaluation parameters without retraining. Based on this, we propose a unified end-to-end framework via a three-class formulation that enables log-likelihood ratio (LLR) inference from class logits for a more interpretable decision pipeline. Experiments show comparable performance to existing methods on ASVSpoof5 and better results on SpoofCeleb. The visualization and analysis also prove that the three-class reformulation provides more interpretability.

♻ ☆ CrossEdit: Cross-Modal Training Enables Rich Audio-Visual Editing
William Chen, Prem Seetharaman, Ke Chen, Oriol Nieto, Kevin Duarte, Siddharth Srinivasan Iyer, Mamshad Nayeem Rizve, Zhiwen Cao, Shinji Watanabe, Yuanjun Xiong, Jianming Zhang, Zeyu Jin, Justin Salamon
Multimedia editing requires generative models to interpret complex, compositional instructions and modify only the desired elements across modalities, a capability largely beyond existing systems. Current approaches are typically limited to simple, single-attribute edits within one modality, since diverse, high-quality editing pairs are hard to obtain, especially for cross-modal tasks where aligned audiovisual (AV) data is scarce. We present CrossEdit, a unified omni-modal editing model for images, audio, and video that performs AV movie scene edits zero-shot through cross-modal transfer. Our key observation is that complex instruction-following, once learned in any modality, generalizes to others. We exploit the additive nature of acoustic signals to procedurally generate large-scale audio editing pairs with compositional instructions, and show that fine-tuning on this synthetic data and self-supervised AV masked reconstruction, alongside a targeted set of curated cross-modal tasks, induces instruction-following that transfers zero-shot to unseen modality and instruction combinations. To evaluate this capability, we release CrossEditBench, a human-annotated benchmark of AV edits on movie scenes, and propose AV-FES, a metric that jointly scores instruction following and consistency. We show that our proposed techniques improve performance on zero-shot AV movie scene editing, while maintaining or improving performance on lip-synced speech editing and standard image, video, and audio editing benchmarks. Demos are available at https://wanchichen.github.io/crossedit/.
