♻ ☆ The Affective Bridge: Preserving Speech Representations while Enhancing Deepfake Detection via emotional Constraints
Yupei Li, Chenyang Lyu, Longyue Wang, Weihua Luo, Kaifu Zhang, Björn W. Schuller
Speech deepfake detection (DFD) has benefited from diverse acoustic and semantic speech representations, many of which encode valuable speech information and are costly to train. Prior work has shown that affective cues improve DFD, yet existing approaches either fuse emotion with other task-specific features in complex pipelines or directly fine-tune representations toward DFD objectives, risking distortion of the original speech representations that support downstream tasks such as speaker verification (SV) or automatic speech recognition (ASR). This preserves the original representation capacity for downstream tasks such as SV and ASR, while emergently improving DFD performance. Crucially, we find that emotion is uniquely effective as this bridging task: replacing it with speaker identity even degrades DFD performance, demonstrating that the benefit stems from emotion's role as a natural bridge between speech representation and DFD. Experiments on FakeOrReal and In-the-Wild show accuracy improvements of up to 6\% and 2\% with corresponding EER reductions, while analysis on ASVspoof 2019 LA reveals dataset-specific speaker bias in the real-speech subset. Code is available at \href{https://github.com/myxp-lyp/The-Affective-Bridge-Unifying-Feature-Representations-for-Speech-Deepfake-Detection}{GitHub repository}.

★ SEMAC: Spherical Energy Matching Ambisonics Codec for Efficient Higher-Order Ambisonics Compression ICASSP 2027
Christoph Hold, Jan Buethe, Jean-Marc Valin, Jan Skoglund, Toni Hirvonen, Nils Peters
Higher-order Ambisonics (HOA) is an attractive format for immersive spatial audio, but its high channel count and directional properties present significant audio coding challenges. The widely deployed Opus audio codec supports HOA through Channel Mapping Families 2 and 3 (RFC 8486), which code and transmit every Ambisonics channel, so the bitrate grows quadratically with the spherical harmonic order. We introduce SEMAC, which instead represents an Ambisonics signal by a quantized full-order directional energy envelope together with fewer CELT-coded transport channels. CELT separates a per-band energy envelope from the signal shape and restores it after quantization, and SEMAC generalizes this principle to directional signals. Since the reduced transport spans only a lower-dimensional subspace, the decoder re-imposes the envelope observed at the encoder input, restoring the directional energy distribution at full order. A MUSHRA test on fifth-order material compares SEMAC against Opus CMF~3 in matched configurations at 512 and 768 kbit/s. SEMAC with 16 of 36 transport channels is rated above full-order CMF~3 at both rates, and at equal transport channel count above order truncation. The proposed SEMAC strategy of coding fewer transport channels with the directional envelope is found perceptually preferable to coding all HOA channels at low precision.

Auditory attention decoding (AAD) seeks to identify the attended talker from brief noninvasive brain recordings by comparing neural responses with competing speech streams. We introduce CoupleFlow, which decodes attention through temporal coupling between neural and acoustic embeddings. Its predictions remain at chance when the brain signal contains no informative coupling, preventing shortcuts based on speech content or talker identity. This rule is Bayes optimal when the recording depends only on the attended talker and removes preferences for speech that is likely a priori. We evaluate CoupleFlow with content disjoint splits recovered from the audio and null tests that distinguish genuine temporal coupling from trial recognition. Across nine EEG and magnetoencephalography (MEG) datasets processed through a common pipeline, spanning four languages, high density EEG recordings, listeners with hearing impairment, and a room with multiple talkers, CoupleFlow outperforms linear and deep baselines while all null tests remain at chance. Finally, we derive an evidence accumulation law that predicts accuracy across window lengths from a single parameter per dataset and predicts that parameter from the strength of neural speech tracking. This law identifies recording signal to noise ratio as a limit on decoding speed and reliability and estimates the window length required to reach a target accuracy.

This paper presents the ICASSP 2026 Radar Acoustic Speech Enhancement (RASE) Grand Challenge, the first community challenge dedicated to benchmarking speech enhancement from millimeter-wave (mmWave) radar vibrometry. The challenge targets realistic through-glass sensing scenarios where microphones are ineffective or impractical. We introduce a curated dataset of paired radar and clean speech recordings, standardized preprocessing, a baseline system, and a secure Codabench-based evaluation framework with unified objective metrics. The RASE Challenge establishes the first public benchmark for radar-based speech enhancement and aims to foster reproducible research in this emerging field.
comment: Published in IEEE ICASSP 2026. Author-accepted manuscript. Challenge resources and code available via the official project website
☆ SURE-Tagger: Structured Speech Representations for Compositional Evaluation and Targeted Data Selection
Jing Peng, Huifei Wang, Weihan Chen, Shuo Gao, Bicheng Zhang, Junhao Du, Hanqi Li, Chaolei Liu, Wen Wen, Tao Liu, Xu Li, Yu Xi, Shuai Wang, Kai Yu
Speech conveys linguistic content, speaker characteristics, temporal interactions, paralinguistic cues, and acoustic environments. While recent speech captioning models describe these dimensions in natural language, inconsistent attribute coverage and ambiguous omissions hinder systematic analysis across recordings. We introduce SURE-Tagger, a framework that constructs semi-structured speech representations with explicit attribute values, supplementary descriptions, and abstention under insufficient evidence. By integrating specialist observations through language-model reasoning, SURE-Tagger enables speech conditions to be consistently identified and jointly queried across datasets. We further introduce Tag-Bench, combining real recordings with controlled, agentically synthesized speech scenes and verified attribute annotations. On Tag-Bench, SURE-Tagger achieves the highest scores on 25 of 29 evaluated dimensions for real speech and 24 of 29 for synthetic speech, outperforming caption-based baselines across structural and descriptive attributes. Beyond annotation, we use these representations to construct cross-dataset evaluation subsets and reveal condition-specific ASR errors. Using a separate candidate pool, SURE-Tagger-guided selection reduces the overall ASR error rate of Qwen3-ASR-1.7B by 14.3% relative to the unadapted model under a one-hour fine-tuning budget, while caption-guided and random selection increase error in the same setting. These results demonstrate how structured speech representations can connect rich annotation, compositional evaluation, and targeted model improvement.
comment: Code will be released at https://github.com/PigeonDan1/sure-tagger
☆ Uni-Stream: A Unified Streaming Speech Language Model for Speech Synthesis and Recognition
Xuan Shi, Chang Zeng, Tiantian Feng, Ye Zhang, Jun Liu, Shih-Heng Wang, Lie Lu, Shrikanth Narayanan
Unified streaming speech language models aim to support speech recognition and synthesis within a single model, enabling real-time human-computer interaction. However, jointly supporting these two directions of speech-text conversion while preserving task-specific performance remains challenging. We propose Uni-Stream, a unified streaming speech language model built on compact pretrained speech models. Uni-Stream processes interleaved text and speech in a streaming format and achieves performance comparable to task-specific models through two-stage training. We also develop a data annotation pipeline for streaming training and will publicly release the generated transcriptions and word-level timestamps. We further examine Uni-Stream's representations across tasks and modalities and find that speech and text residence in distinct latent feature space even when trained in a unified model architecture, while representations within each modality become more task-dependent in later layers.
☆ MG-REPA: Multi-Granularity Representation Alignment for Generative Target Speaker Extraction
Dohwan Kim, Jung-Woo Choi
Generative target speaker extraction (TSE) models achieve high-quality extraction, but suffer from considerably slow training convergence. Representation Alignment (REPA) accelerates diffusion transformer training by aligning hidden states with a pre-trained Self-Supervised Learning (SSL) teacher. However, existing alignment in the speech and audio domain operates at a single granularity. For TSE, frame-level alignment leaves the global, time-invariant characteristics of the target speech implicit, whereas utterance-level alignment leaves the time-varying content implicit, even though extracting the target requires both. We propose Multi-Granularity Representation Alignment (MG-REPA), aligning the hidden states with an SSL model at the frame level and a speaker verification model at the utterance level. We further apply temporal normalization to the frame-level target, removing its utterance-level statistics so that each branch concentrates on its granularity. On Libri2Mix, MG-REPA reaches the OVRL and PESQ of a MeanFlow-TSE baseline with $3.0\times$ and $2.1\times$ fewer epochs, respectively. Trained for 750 epochs, it is competitive with the published 2,000-epoch baseline on intrusive metrics while improving non-intrusive metrics. An ablation demonstrates that MG-REPA outperforms alignment at a single granularity.
☆ NECTAR: Automatic Negative Clue Estimation via Centroid-Space Mapping for Target Speaker Extraction
Hyungjun Yoo, Yongjoon Lee, Jung-Woo Choi
Target speaker extraction (TSE) aims to extract a desired speaker from a mixture using auxiliary clues such as enrollment speech. An interferer-related representation can provide a useful negative clue for TSE, but such information is not directly available from the target enrollment. To derive this representation from the observed mixture, we analyze the relationship between the speaker representations of a speech mixture and its constituent speakers. Our analysis shows that the mixture centroid lies near the midpoint of its constituent speaker centroids, whereas this relationship does not hold for single-utterance embeddings. Based on this observation, we propose NECTAR, NEgative Clue for TARget speaker extraction, which automatically derives an interferer-related negative clue from the mixture using the centroid-space relationship. We further introduce a Centroid-Space Mapper (CSM) to estimate the required centroid representations from a mixture and a target enrollment. NECTAR achieves the highest SI-SDRi on Libri2Mix among the compared systems trained on LibriSpeech train-clean-100, reaching 16.18 dB.
☆ Concentrated Causal Influence, Distributed Diagnostic Information: Cognitive Impairment Decisions in Large Audio-Language Models
Xiutian Zhao, Luqi Sun, Björn Schuller, Berrak Sisman
Large audio-language models (LALMs) can assess cognitive impairment (CI) from speech, yet their answers reveal neither which internal components control the decision nor how much CI information is accessible in their representations. We investigate both questions through CI-contrast neurons (CICNs), selected by class-contrastive activation frequency in decoder MLPs. Across eight open LALMs and two corpora (Pitt and PROCESS-2), we causally test CICNs against size- and layer-matched random masks and activity-matched controls. In three of the five models that meet our eligibility criteria, ablation of small CICN sets causes large, class-directed prediction shifts; speech-identified masks also control transcript-only decisions, and three of four primary Pitt masks retain specificity on PROCESS-2. Position-restricted interventions locate the influence before the final answer position, most strongly after the speech or transcript evidence under letter-labeled options, largely as a decision-direction shift. Beyond causal localization, supervised linear readouts of frozen CICN activations achieve 0.92--0.97 AUC within Pitt, versus 0.67--0.84 for the models' direct answers. Matched random and all-neuron readouts reach comparable performance; top-ranked CICNs show only an exploratory advantage at very small unit budgets. These results distinguish concentrated causal control over output decisions from broadly distributed diagnostic information for CI detection in LALMs.
☆ X-Dubbing: Speech-to-Speech Translation under Temporal and Visual Constraints
Jeongsoo Choi, Ji-Hoon Kim, Junseok Ahn, Joon Son Chung
Cross-lingual dubbing aims to convert source speech into target-language speech that remains synchronized with the original video. The key to this task is to produce a faithful translation that is naturally speakable within the source timing, which is non-trivial because languages differ in duration, rhythm, and articulation. In this paper, we propose X-Dubbing, which formulates the task as a joint problem of time-aware speech-to-text translation and video-aware text-to-speech. Specifically, our method consists of a Dubbing Translator that generates temporally structured scripts and a Voice Actor that renders them in synchrony with the source video, both grounded in a language-agnostic timing budget. We further refine the translator with dubbing-aware feedback from the synthesized speech, encouraging scripts that yield well-synchronized dubbing. This design requires no paired dubbing data, as the two components are trained on speech-text and monolingual audio-visual data respectively. Extensive experiments show that X-Dubbing outperforms recent baselines across diverse metrics, including isochrony and audio-visual correspondence.
☆ Beyond Visible Speakers: Context-Aware Active Speaker Detection with Speaker Registration ICASSP 2027
Pu Wang, Hugo Van hamme
Active speaker detection (ASD) relies on audiovisual correspondence between speech and visible faces, yet this correspondence becomes unreliable in crowded scenes, or when visual evidence is unavailable. We introduce ROAM-ASD-C and ROAM-ASD-CR to extend ROAM-ASD with contextual and identity-aware reasoning. ROAM-ASD-C jointly reasons across simultaneously visible candidates, allowing other faces to provide complementary evidence when the target observation is ambiguous or incomplete. ROAM-ASD-CR incorporates registered-speaker representations derived from enrollment speech, allowing detection of whether a speaker is active even when that speaker is not visually observed. ROAM-ASD-C achieves state-of-the-art performance across five ASD benchmarks: 96.8% mAP on AVA, 98.9% on WASD, 88.8% on UniTalk, 98.7% on Talkies, and 99.5% on ASW. It also improves ROAM-ASD by up to 13.3 mAP under 75% target-track visual removal.
comment: Submitted to IEEE ICASSP 2027
☆ JIT-MPE: Just-in-Time Multi-Pitch Estimation under Output Deadlines
Yoshiyuki Kobayashi
Live pitch displays, score followers and accompaniment systems must know which pitches are sounding within tens of milliseconds, but instrument-agnostic multi-pitch estimation (MPE) has mainly been designed and evaluated offline. We present JIT-MPE, a causal MPE model of 86k parameters for mixed ensembles. It gives an immediate estimate of each 20 ms frame and re-estimates the same frame as 20, 40, 80 and 160 ms of further audio arrive, so that a live display can show pitches at once and then refine them. We score each output only at a deadline by which it can be computed from the audio that has arrived, on five development sets and four held-out sets evaluated only after all design choices were frozen. At a 50 ms deadline, which reads the update made with 40 ms of lookahead, JIT-MPE is significantly more accurate than five of six published offline MPE systems in 38 of 45 comparisons (15 of 20 on the held-out sets) and less accurate in only two, although these systems read the whole recording and all but one have 6 to 170 times as many parameters; the sixth, supervised on URMP, is higher on four of the nine sets. The deadline costs little: on the held-out sets, JIT-MPE at 50 ms is within $-1.27$ to $+0.60$ points of recording-level macro F1 of its own final output with 160 ms of lookahead and within $-2.08$ to $+0.79$ points of a bidirectional model of similar size. Waiting pays off where the immediate estimate is weakest: the update at 50 ms adds 1.7-3.6 points over it on the development data and three of the four held-out sets, and raises the recall of reference frames in the first 20 ms after a note onset from 9.8% to 38.4% on the held-out AAM set. The slowest measured frame takes at most 4.15 ms on one CPU thread. Code and trained weights are available at https://github.com/Frieve-A/jit-mpe.
comment: 18 pages, 3 figures. Code and trained weights: https://github.com/Frieve-A/jit-mpe
♻ ☆ Commanding at the Speed of Sound: Audio-Centric Referring Expression Segmentation for Aerial Scenes
Ziyun Chen, Yijun Wang, Chuanyi Zhang, Liang Yao, Yuexuan An, Xiang Gu, Wei Zhou, Fan Liu
Referring expression segmentation (RES) aims to localize targets at the pixel level guided by human instructions. However, current models predominantly follow a text-centric paradigm that treats discrete text as the primary interaction medium for these human instructions. This assumption is especially limiting in unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) applications, where rapid response, hands-free operation, and natural communication are often critical. In this paper, we reconstruct UAV referring expression segmentation through an audio-centric perspective. Grounded in information theory, we demonstrate that raw audio provides a higher upper bound for extracting rich semantic features than transcribed text. To achieve this, we construct an audio-driven UAV referring expression segmentation benchmark named Aerial-AudioRES by augmenting VisDrone with synthesized speech, forming "audio-text-image-mask" quadruples. Specifically, we employ an ambiguity filtering mechanism to ensure referential uniqueness, and incorporate eight distinct timbres alongside 4 realistic noises to simulate authentic environments. To drive the paradigm shift from text-centric to audio-centric, we propose the end-to-end Audio-centric Referring Expression Segmentation Network (ARES-Net). Distinct from discrete text-visual matching, our approach learns to establish a direct soft alignment between continuous acoustic manifolds and multi-scale visual representations. Comprehensive experiments show that our method obtains a peak accuracy of 64.23% in oIoU and demonstrates robust generalization on a collected real-human test set. Furthermore, it significantly reduces total interaction latency to one-third of the text-based method. Our code is available at https://github.com/LemonGauss/ARES-Net.
♻ ☆ AU-Harness: An Open-Source Toolkit for Efficient and Unified Evaluation of AUdio-LLMs EMNLP 2026
Hoang Nguyen, Sidharth Surapaneni, Akshay Kalkunte, Jash Mehta, Aman Tiwari, Oluwanifemi Bamgbose, Khyati Mahajan, Jash Shah, Shruthan Radhakrishna, Sathwik Tejaswi Madhusudhan, Vikas Yadav, Sai Rajeswar
Large Audio Language Models (LALMs) are rapidly advancing, but evaluating them remains challenging due to inefficient and nonstandardized toolkits that limit fair comparison and systematic assessment. Existing evaluation frameworks exhibit three critical limitations: (1) slow and inefficient processing pipeline that bottlenecks large-scale studies, (2) inadequate multi-turn dialogue support, leaving fundamental questions about cross-turn context integration and performance dynamics over extended conversations in LALMs unanswered; and (3) the absence of unified and scalable evaluation framework capable of keeping pace with the rapid growth of both LALMs and audio benchmarks. To address these issues, we introduce AU-Harness, an efficient and comprehensive evaluation framework for LALMs. Our empirical studies demonstrate that AU-Harness achieves 77% reduction in evaluation processing time over existing evaluation toolkits, enabling large-scale LALM evaluations previously considered impractical. We provide standardized evaluation protocols and flexible configurations for fair model comparison across diverse scenarios. AU-Harness unlocks a range of in-depth analyses difficult to conduct without a unified foundation, including multi-turn dialogue dynamics, enabling the study of true audio reasoning capabilities in existing LALMs. AU-Harness provides both practical evaluation tools and insights into model limitations, advancing systematic LALM development.
comment: EMNLP 2026 Findings
Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition 150
☆ SceneBloom: Agentic Indoor Environment Generation with Realistic and Diverse Layouts for Embodied Learning
Yuhan Liu, Lianhui Qin, Shenji Wan
Training generalizable embodied agents requires realistic, varied, and simulation-ready indoor environments. Language-guided methods support semantic planning and object-level reasoning, but precise spatial grounding remains difficult. Visual generative models offer rich priors over plausible arrangements, yet their outputs require geometric reasoning to become physically valid 3D scenes. We introduce SceneBloom, an agentic framework that combines visual layout sampling with contract-guided 3D compilation. A hierarchical sampler uses diffusion priors to generate furniture arrangements within functional zones. A compiler then uses relations extracted from each proposal to guide geometric fitting and local pose correction. Across five room types, SceneBloom attains the highest visual quality and physical stability among the compared methods and is the only method with no detected mesh collisions and out-of-bounds objects. Its layouts are also closer to the distribution of real rooms than those of all compared baselines. Object navigation policies trained in these realistic scenes achieve a higher success rate in held-out real scans than those trained on an equal number of real training scans. Code is available at https://github.com/Tinaliu0123/scenebloom.
☆ UniAction: Unified Action Conditioning for World Models
Bowen Xue, Zizhang Li, Hong-Xing Yu, Jiajun Wu
Actions that condition world models are highly heterogeneous, and thus existing action-conditioned world models are typically built for individual action types, fragmenting already limited action-annotated data across separate models. We introduce UniAction, a unified action-conditioning framework that represents any action as a sparse set of action elements, each with a discrete semantic identity and a continuous spatiotemporal grounding coordinate. By mapping these coordinates directly into the pretrained video model's native positional space, UniAction allows heterogeneous actions to condition a shared world model within the same spatiotemporal structure. We further introduce cardinality-calibrated attention to address the bias from differing action representation granularities. We evaluate UniAction on four representative action forms: force, camera control, hand pose, and robot pose. UniAction outperforms conditioning alternatives in action following, and a single jointly trained model surpasses the action-specific experts, showing that heterogeneous action data benefit from unified model and joint training.
comment: Project page: https://uniaction.github.io/
☆ FlexGlue: Sparse-to-Dense Feature Matching and Visual Disambiguation
Philipp Lindenberger, Paul-Edouard Sarlin, Ondrej Miksik, Marc Pollefeys
To estimate correspondences across images, existing approaches match either sparse interest points, which is highly efficient but limited by repeatability, or dense pixel grids, which is robust but expensive. Furthermore, these approaches are trained with only matching pairs and thus often fail to reject unrelated pairs that exhibit visual symmetries, which is equally important in applications like Structure-from-Motion (SfM). We bridge these gaps by introducing FlexGlue, a neural network for asymmetric sparse-to-dense matching and disambiguation. Given two images and coordinates of points in the first image, FlexGlue estimates the coordinates of the corresponding points in the second image while simultaneously rejecting the pair if non-matching. By searching for a limited set of correspondences among dense pixels, our approach is both fast and effective at both matching and disambiguation: it combines the sub-pixel accuracy of dense matching with the speed of sparse matching, while rejecting incorrect pairs with high precision. Experiments on multiple datasets show that FlexGlue pushes the Pareto frontier in relative pose estimation and significantly outperforms existing approaches for SfM and visual localization. FlexGlue is publicly available at https://github.com/cvg/flexglue .
☆ MiD-VLM: Detecting and Grounding Global Semantic Misinformation in Image-Caption Pairs
Tarunya Prasad, Bharatesh Chakravarthi
Semantic misinformation can arise when an authentic image is paired with a caption that changes or distorts its narrative. Because the image itself may contain no visible signs of manipulation, methods designed to detect pixel-level artifacts can miss these misleading image-caption pairs. We study this problem using DGM4+, a dataset designed to evaluate the detection of global scene and semantic inconsistencies. We propose a multimodal model that combines image-text representations from SigLIP with visual scene features from DINOv2 through a projection MLP, and adapts Qwen2-VL-7B using LoRA. The model jointly predicts whether an image-caption pair is authentic, identifies the manipulation type, and grounds the misleading caption tokens. On the DGM4+ validation split, the model achieves an F1 score of $0.9679$ for binary authenticity classification. These results suggest that parameter-efficient adaptation of vision-language models is promising for detecting semantic inconsistencies, while also motivating further work on precise token-level grounding.
☆ ViT-H: Generative Video-To-Humanoid Control with Motion Tracking Feedback
Zimo He, Tianyi Bian, Zizhong Yang, Hongjie Li, Nan Jiang, Jieming Cui, Baoxiong Jia, Yizhou Wang, Siyuan Huang, Yixin Zhu
Learning humanoid control from monocular human videos offers a scalable way to acquire diverse whole-body behaviors. Yet, existing reconstruction-retargeting-tracking pipelines are limited in system-level scalability by separately optimized intermediate stages and cannot directly optimize reference motion executability using downstream tracking feedback. We present ViT-H, a video-to-humanoid control framework following a generation-and-tracking paradigm. ViT-H directly generates humanoid reference motions from videos with a diffusion model, bypassing human motion reconstruction and retargeting, and uses motion-tracking outcomes to post-train the generator with direct preference optimization. We further introduce an autoregressive variant that enables real-time humanoid video teleoperation with sub-400 ms latency. Extensive experiments on the Unitree G1 demonstrate that ViT-H outperforms state-of-the-art reconstruction-retargeting-tracking pipelines in both motion quality and executability. We further show that ViT-H scales favorably with model size and with both pre-training and post-training data scale, while motion-tracking feedback consistently improves executability across different motion trackers.
comment: The first four authors contributed equally. Project website: https://awfuact.github.io/vit-h/
☆ Flownomaly: Single-Step Conditional-Mean Recovery for Few-Shot Anomaly Detection
Bernardo Perrone Ribeiro, Erkut Akdag, Egor Bondarev
Few-shot industrial anomaly detection requires modeling category-specific normality from only a handful of defect-free images. Common approaches tie inference to stored exemplars, impose rigid linear structure, or risk reproducing anomalous content. Flownomaly instead casts the problem as normal-counterpart recovery in frozen DINOv2 feature space. Given normal supports, a velocity field is learned through conditional flow matching over frozen patch tokens to transport Gaussian noise toward normal features. Along straight paths, a single recovery step using one evaluation of the optimal field yields the posterior mean of the clean normal token without trajectory integration. The operating time governs how strongly recovery modifies a query token. With no anomalous validation samples available for tuning, a normal-only Jacobian gain-to-noise criterion selects this time from the supports alone. Squared residuals between query tokens and their recovered counterparts yield anomaly signals for both dense localization and image-level detection. Across 1-, 2-, and 4-shot benchmarks on MVTec-AD and VisA, together with sample-shot evaluations on Real-IAD, Flownomaly achieves state-of-the-art performance against recent category-specific methods. In the 1-shot setting, image- and pixel-level AUROC reach 97.8% and 98.0% on MVTec-AD and 95.3% and 98.7% on VisA, with a 2.1-point image-level AUROC improvement over the strongest baseline on VisA. Code is available at https://github.com/b-rbmp/Flownomaly.
comment: Accepted to WACV 2027
☆ Beyond Discrete Tokens: Preserving Numerical Continuity in Medical Vision-Language Models
Dianye Huang, Jiamei Guo, Yue Zhou, Mingde Li, Yi Xiong, Wei Wang, Nassir Navab, Zhongliang Jiang
Objective: To develop a unified vision-language model for prompt-conditioned quantitative ultrasound measurement that addresses the mismatch between continuous measurement targets and discrete token-based numerical prediction. Methods: This article presents HAD-VLM, a hybrid autoregressive-diffusion framework that combines autoregressive text generation with continuous measurement prediction within a shared backbone. Visual prompt tuning adapts the vision encoder to ultrasound images. A diffusion process predicts a five-component representation comprising caliper endpoint coordinates and measurement length. A post-processing strategy combining the proposed coordinate-length consistency mechanism with ensemble prediction is introduced to refine measurement estimates. We evaluate four echocardiographic measurement tasks on EchoNet-LVH, with additional assessments of medical question answering and X-ray vertebral measurement. Results: HAD-VLM achieves mean absolute errors of 1.36, 2.77, 3.05, and 1.16 mm for IVSd, LVIDd, LVIDs, and LVPWd, respectively, reducing errors by 21.4-37.6\% relative to the Vicuna-based autoregressive baseline. It also outperforms fine-tuned Qwen3-VL and direct MLP regression across all four tasks. Medical question answering performance is preserved on the evaluated dataset. For X-ray vertebral measurement, HAD-VLM reduces mean absolute error from 11.4 to 6.7 pixels. Conclusion: Integrating autoregressive language generation with diffusion-based continuous prediction improves quantitative medical image measurement while retaining prompt-conditioned task flexibility. Significance: HAD-VLM provides a unified approach to combining language interaction with anatomically grounded numerical prediction for quantitative medical image analysis.
☆ STROKE: Simple Sparse Structural Occlusions for Black-Box Adversarial Attacks
Ankit Gupta, Akshat Pandya, Paul Lin, Christoph Adami, Emily Dolson
We introduce STROKE, a query-efficient score-based black-box adversarial attack that constructs perturbations from simple oriented rectangular occlusions. STROKE optimizes these perturbations through a lightweight greedy add-and-refine procedure. Across diverse image classifiers, STROKE achieves high attack success with low query counts at nominal 1--2\% area settings, showing favorable performance relative to existing patch-based attacks in several configurations. Matched comparisons further demonstrate substantial reductions in wall-clock attack time, while ablation studies examine the key design choices and effectiveness across structural primitives. These findings suggest that simple structural occlusions offer an effective and computationally efficient search space for black-box adversarial attacks.
comment: 13 pages, 4 figures, 4 tables, and 16 pages of Supplementary Information with 3 figures and 5 tables
☆ LoCA: Enabling Multi-Modality in Geospatial Location Encoders
Panagiotis Koromilas, Eleanna Vali, Diogenis Antonopoulos, Eleni Saka, Dimitris Christofis, Nikolaos Ioannis Bountos, Konstantin Klemmer, Ioannis Papoutsis, Yannis Panagakis, Mihalis A. Nicolaou
Location encoders map geographic coordinates to high-dimensional descriptors through contrastive alignment with paired Earth Observation imagery. We prove that this construction is structurally limited: any Lipschitz location encoder produces an output of intrinsic dimension at most 2, regardless of architecture or bandwidth, which forces the contrastive loss to strictly exceed its asymptotic optimum. Empirically, joint training also collapses the encoder's embedding covariance to low rank. Although dimension-limited, current location encoders sidestep this spectral collapse by training against a frozen image encoder, which we reinterpret as a covariance regularizer that supplies a high-rank target for the location encoder to fold onto. However, extending this approach to multimodal inputs is challenging, as location encoders should simultaneously map a single location to multiple, potentially incompatible, descriptors. We identify two requirements a regularizer must satisfy for location encoding in multimodal regimes: co-alignment across modalities, since adapters alone cannot align independently pretrained encoders; and high effective rank, since the location encoder inherits its target's spectrum. We propose LoCA (Location Contrastive Alignment), a two-stage pipeline that satisfies both. Stage 1 jointly trains Sentinel-1 and Sentinel-2 encoders with contrastive learning, producing a co-aligned, high-rank multimodal target. Stage 2 freezes the image encoders and trains a location and a tabular metadata encoder as projection adapters with multi-view contrastive learning. Against five state-of-the-art encoders on 17 tasks ranging from land cover and wildfire forecasting to geophysical, socio-economic, biodiversity and climate applications, LoCA achieves the most task wins, is the only model to outperform every other on a majority of tasks, and wins 68.8% of all per-task comparisons.
☆ Closing the Modality Gap via Simplex-Constrained Representations
Shubham Gupta, Siva Reddy, Perouz Taslakian, Valentina Zantedeschi, Cem Subakan
While multimodal contrastive models like CLIP and CLAP successfully learn shared representations, their embeddings typically exhibit a persistent \emph{modality gap}. We propose addressing this separation through a purely geometric approach: changing the embedding domain from the unit sphere, $S^{d-1}$, to the probability simplex, $Δ^{d-1}$. Although both manifolds share the same intrinsic dimension, the simplex acts as a structural prior; its nonnegative, unit-mass constraints serve as a cross-modal calibration that forces both modalities to ground themselves in the same coordinate system. By attaching lightweight softmax adapters and using Total Variation similarity, we reduce the centroid $\ell_2$ gap by 97--99\% across five multimodal retrieval benchmarks. This confirms that simplicial geometry induces genuine semantic alignment, matching or exceeding the retrieval performance of standard unconstrained models.
☆ VTRL-Med: Progressive Visual Refinement with Topology-Guided Regularization for Medical Image Clustering
Guangyu Meng, Pengfei Gu, Peixian Liang, John P. Lalor, Erin Wolf Chambers, Danny Z. Chen
Deep clustering offers a promising approach for analyzing large unlabeled medical image datasets, yet prevailing methods still face two limitations: they may neglect class-agnostic structural priors that capture object boundaries and regions, and they do not explicitly encode topological patterns (e.g., connectivity and holes). These sources of information play distinct and complementary roles: visual-structural features provide the primary discriminative representation for clustering, while topological features provide additional global geometric cues for residual visual ambiguities. We introduce VTRL-Med, a progressive visual-structural learning framework with topology-guided regularization for medical image clustering. VTRL-Med first adapts the Segment Anything Model (SAM) to extract image features that retain structural cues inherited from mask-supervised pretraining. It then generates reliable pseudo-labels through a two-step filtering process that combines prototype-based selection with k-nearest neighbor consistency validation. Finally, it progressively refines the visual branch while an auxiliary topology branch, constructed from persistent homology (PH) descriptors, provides additional geometric regularization during training. Across 13 medical image benchmarks, VTRL-Med achieves state-of-the-art clustering performance, improving average accuracy by 4.48% over existing methods. On three representative datasets, topology-guided regularization further improves accuracy by 1.3--4.3% over visual refinement alone.
☆ Multimodal Generative AI Assists Comprehensive Echocardiographic Interpretation
Yi Qin, Marawan Elbatel, Shanshan Song, Taoran Huang, Jiarong Guo, Ningshu Li, Lehan Wang, Chenxu Zhao, Jiexin He, Machteld J. Boonstra, Stephan van der Zwaard, Marielle C. van de Veerdonk, Pere Lopez-Gutierrez, Lydia Dux-Santoy, Andrea Guala, Enrique Almar-Munoz, Sebastian Johannes Reinstadler, Radek Debiec, Yi-Hang Zhu, Huiyu Zhou, Adrian P Cheong, Yike Guo, Agnes Mayr, Karim Lekadir, Yong Jiang, Nilesh J. Samani, Dacheng Tao, Folkert W. Asselbergs, Hongwen Fei, Alex PW Lee, Xiaomeng Li
Echocardiography is the cornerstone of cardiovascular diagnostics, yet its global utility is constrained by a critical shortage of experienced interpreters. Current artificial intelligence (AI) solutions remain limited, typically operating as opaque "black boxes" or focusing on narrow tasks that fail to capture the holistic, guideline-driven reasoning of a clinician. Here we introduce EchoChat, a generative multimodal vision-language model that performs comprehensive echocardiographic analysis to support clinician interpretation. By emulating the cognitive workflow of a cardiologist, EchoChat integrates vast medical knowledge with a chain-of-thought reasoning mechanism to explicitly ground its conclusions in visual evidence. Trained on echocardiography-instruction pairs from 46,358 examinations, our model establishes a new state-of-the-art across diverse cohorts from six international medical centers. It supports the broadest diagnostic scope of 33 cardiac conditions and findings, including 15 newly added conditions for which it achieves an average F1 of 73.7% across available external evaluations. It surpasses existing best-performing foundation models in cardiac condition recognition (improving average recall by 13.54% on shared tasks) and quantification (average R2 score increase of 0.275 on shared tasks). Furthermore, in a source-blinded echocardiographer reader study, echocardiography reports co-generated with EchoChat were rated higher in diagnostic accuracy and completeness by two senior echocardiographers, and improved diagnostic performance from 72.78% to 82.75% in terms of F1 score over routine-reader only reports. These results demonstrate that integrating clinical reasoning into multimodal AI can democratize specialist expertise and transform the standard of cardiovascular care.
☆ OpenStripe supports open-set identification and spatial stripe profiling in wild Amur tigers
Yichun Peng, Yansong Li, Jin Hou, Qi Song, Xi Guo, Ning Zhang, Degang Wei, Huang Yang, Yu Guan, Jianping Ge, Lei Bao, Tianming Wang
Non-invasive camera-trap monitoring of endangered wildlife requires open-set individual identification---grouping field images into identities without predefined classes or a known population size---yet pose deformation and cluttered backgrounds complicate image comparison. Here, we present OpenStripe, a multi-agent framework that reconstructs canonical two-dimensional (2D) tiger torso patterns and encodes four interpretable local stripe structures: breakpoints, bifurcations, irregular structures, and round structures. We evaluated OpenStripe on 100 camera-trap records from 28 wild Amur tigers (Panthera tigris altaica), representing nearly one-third of the documented population in the Northeast China Tiger and Leopard National Park. Combining all four complementary structures enabled automatic identity grouping with 0.90 matched accuracy and a 0.85 adjusted Rand index (ARI), outperforming 49 baseline configurations under the same backend (up to 0.43 accuracy and 0.14 ARI). To display a desired appearance, PM typically uses projector compensation, which computes a projector input that counteracts the geometric and photometric distortions of the scene. Compensation can only approximate this appearance within the available projection range, and it cannot revise the appearance itself. Pretrained LLM-based image editors provide a direct way to produce the desired appearance from a text prompt or reference image; projector compensation can then attempt to reproduce the edited result through projection. However, these editors do not have an accurate measure of the scene geometry or scene response. To address this problem, we introduce SREdit, an efficient response-guided framework for projection-based appearance editing. SREdit estimates a scene response map from the reconstructed scene that reflects how strongly projected illumination can affect different surface regions. SREdit uses the source appearance to constrain the early sampling process and preserve registration with the fixed physical object, while the scene response map adapts the amount of editing across surface regions. Experiments across two pretrained image editors show that SREdit improves projected appearance quality and reproduction fidelity. It adds less than one second per image with negligible VRAM overhead. Participants also consistently preferred the results produced with SREdit in our user study.

Furthermore, we introduce a composite loss to improve background-target separation. This loss integrates constrained energy minimization loss to enhance target saliency and suppress the background by maximizing the target response while minimizing average output energy, alongside binary cross-entropy loss to classify background and target using pixel-wise labels. We further introduce a Multi-Ring Spherical Convolution that aggregates neighboring pixels over a nearly uniform spherical receptive field across latitudes. Experiments on a public omnidirectional image dataset demonstrate BD-rate reductions of 16.3%, 26.5%, and 19.5% over VVC in terms of V-PSNR, V-MS-SSIM, and V-LPIPS, respectively. Our method also achieves a 13.1% BD-rate reduction over ERP-based Cool-Chic 5.0 in terms of V-PSNR, while providing 2.6-3.6x faster decoding than the evaluated learned autoencoder codecs.

Continuous Piecewise-Affine Based (CPAB) transformations, introduced by Freifeld et al. (2015, 2017), are flows obtained by integrating continuous piecewise-affine (CPA) velocity fields. These expressive transformations have proven useful in applications including nonlinear temporal warping and trainable activation functions in 1D, as well as nonrigid spatial deformations in 2D and 3D. While computational costs were not an issue in 1D, they originally limited the practical expressiveness of CPAB transformations in higher dimensions, especially in 3D. Our recent work (Aflalo et al., 2026) removed this bottleneck, enabling efficient optimization with much finer tessellations and substantially greater expressiveness. There is, however, a mathematical subtlety that was overlooked in the original CPAB papers (Freifeld et al., 2015, 2017). CPAB transformations are always bi-Lipschitz homeomorphisms, implying that both the transformations and their inverses are differentiable almost everywhere. They are not, however, necessarily diffeomorphisms. This note remedies the omission by identifying sufficient regularity conditions under which a CPAB transformation is guaranteed to be a diffeomorphism. We explain how differentiability can fail and how the proposed conditions prevent this failure. In 1D and 2D, we show that these conditions can be easily enforced and, for commonly used tessellations, hold with probability one under standard sampling assumptions. We expect analogous behavior in 3D.

We present MoST, a black-box testing framework that characterizes modality sensitivity by comparing image-only, text-only, and joint perturbations. The models exhibit distinct sensitivities: textual perturbations dominate for some, whereas others are susceptible across both modalities. In several configurations, joint perturbations match or exceed the effectiveness of single-modality perturbations with smaller modifications to each input. In a human study, 60-76% of assessments across models judge the perturbed inputs sufficiently understandable to perform the task, and human localization is more accurate than that of the corresponding VLMs. These results show that evaluating modalities separately can overlook failure-inducing combinations and that modality sensitivity provides a more detailed account of VLM robustness than aggregate failure rates alone.

Existing methods can generate orderly and rhythmically synchronized group motion, but remain limited in formation evolution and inter-dancer interaction. In human choreography, formation transitions often align with changes in high-level musical structure, such as the progression from an introduction to a chorus or from a chorus to a climax. We present ChoreoStudio, which makes choreography planning explicit. A music disentangler first decomposes the audio into frame-level rhythmic features and segment-level structural features. Given the segment-level features and sparse labels, a frozen omni-modal model acts as a scriptwriter, producing a global semantic description that guides the Director's choreography planning. Based on this context, the Director produces three coupled interaction decisions: a centroid-relative point set specifies what formation to produce, a transition gate determines when it should change, and a mobility allocation indicates who should execute the transition. The transition gate and mobility allocation are further conditioned on the planned geometric change, coupling formation targets with their temporal and dancer-specific execution. At a finer temporal scale, frame-aligned music features condition the diffusion generator to control detailed body motion and preserve beat-level alignment. The segment-level interaction plan is injected in parallel through frame-aligned instruction tokens and cross-dancer attention biases, coordinating how the generator realizes each transition. Experiments on AIOZ-GDance demonstrate that ChoreoStudio follows the planned interactions while achieving state-of-the-art performance in motion quality, group organization, and formation dynamics.

To address this problem, we propose DeformStruct, an instance-level deformable structure modeling framework for PTAL. DeformStruct progressively constructs the structure of each action instance through three stages. Second, Deformable Part Alignment associates latent structural parts with these anchors through deformation-aware matching, allowing their temporal supports to adapt to instance-dependent variations. Existing methods typically perform video-text alignment in Euclidean space, where representations are embedded in a flat geometry. However, accurate moment localization requires organizing query-relevant evidence across multiple grounding states, where target regions, boundary transitions, and contextual distractors exhibit distinct temporal structures and relevance patterns. Specifically, we propose Hyperbolic Temporal Evidence Organization (HTEO), a geometric framework that organizes query-aware temporal memory in hyperbolic space. REO adjusts temporal tokens' radial positions to encode the structural differences among temporal evidence, while OAR enhances query-conditioned semantic alignment through orthogonal rotation. Furthermore, we introduce radial structure regularization and angular relevance supervision to explicitly guide temporal evidence organization and query-conditioned semantic alignment, respectively. Extensive experiments and analyses across multiple benchmarks demonstrate that HTEO improves temporal localization while providing an interpretable geometric organization of temporal evidence.

While DINO's invariance-based training could absorb this pixel-level mixing into clean features, experiments with over 26K foreground patches show it does not: boundary-overlapping patches produce features with higher entropy and lower assignment confidence, blurring predicted part boundaries. Rather than make the massive effort of retraining DINO over geometrically coherent regions, an easier approach is to take boundaries directly from a boundary detector, which supplies the geometric information DINO's features lack. Motivated by this, we introduce Part-DINO, a training-free framework that combines boundaries from low-level image segmentation with DINO's semantic features. We use the boundaries to partition the image into regions, pool DINO features within each region, and group them to discover parts. Without any training, Part-DINO produces structurally coherent part assignments, outperforming training-free baselines across four standard benchmarks (CUB, CelebA, PartImageNet-OOD, PartImageNet-Seg) and remaining competitive with weakly-supervised and unsupervised methods.

Fixed-window Vision Transformer (ViT) decoders run at deployment resolution as overlapping tiles: every token in an overlap band is processed by several full decoder instances. In the 2.4B-parameter MiniMax-H3 video decoder, about half of all per-token computation is duplicated. Removing the tiles fails because attention, global tokens and coordinates are bound to them. TileShare keeps each released tile's attention and computes every other operation once per token. Without training, keeping six layers per tile decodes 1.38-1.51x faster than batched and compiled tiling on two GPU types (up to 1.96x with FP8) and is equivalent to the released decoder in PSNR, LPIPS and DISTS on DAVIS videos. On unseen UVG videos with the setting frozen beforehand, it matches PSNR and DISTS and improves LPIPS. TileShare carries over to two further decoders and is again confirmed on unseen data. It is equivalent in PSNR and DISTS on MAGI-1. On the ViTok-v2 image autoencoder at 2K-4K, it matches overlapping tiling in PSNR, improves LPIPS and DISTS and decodes 1.5-1.8x faster. How many layers stay per tile is measured once per model (for decoders, without labels); we report it for 14 decoders and encoders. Optionally, two GPU-hours of self-distillation let MiniMax-H3 share every layer without a loss in PSNR, and a coordinate field trained while the network stays frozen brings fully shared CLIP-based open-vocabulary segmentation to parity with sliding windows on seven benchmarks.

Despite their success, the robustness of these models against adversarial camouflage attacks remains largely unexplored. Existing camouflage attacks primarily target single-view 2D detectors, limiting their effectiveness in multi-view 3D perception settings. To address this gap, we propose BEVCA, a novel adversarial camouflage generation framework tailored for multi-view BEV-based 3D perception. Our framework integrates a BEV-feature-based adversarial loss with a multi-view neural rendering module, enabling effective and transferable camouflage attacks across different models and tasks. Extensive experiments in both digital and physical settings demonstrate that BEVCA outperforms state-of-the-art baselines and exhibits strong robustness under real-world conditions. Realizing this potential requires reward signals that reliably rank videos by both VQ and AF. However, existing rewards capture only one dimension: metric-based rewards assess VQ but require ground-truth videos and do not directly assess AF, while inverse dynamics model (IDM) rewards assess AF without references but do not guarantee VQ. Moreover, IDMs, typically trained on real videos, may provide unreliable rewards for generated videos containing visual artifacts and physical inconsistencies. In this work, we introduce the Action and Video Mismatch Benchmark (AVM-Eval), comprising 67.2k pairs that evaluate how reliably IDMs assess AF on real and generated videos. We then propose ACWM-RM, a reward model that jointly assesses VQ and AF without ground-truth videos during reward computation. To train it, we first construct the Action and Video Mismatch Preference Dataset (AVM-Pref) with 506.3k pairs providing complementary supervision: action-mismatch pairs supervise AF, while video-mismatch pairs supervise VQ and expose the model to generated videos. We then pretrain an action-conditioned predictor on real videos to learn forward dynamics before jointly training it with a patch-weighted score head on AVM-Pref to transfer these dynamics to AF assessment on generated videos. Using threshold decomposition, we construct a neural disjunctive normal form representation and establish a sufficient condition for exactness with integer-valued images and structuring elements. We then derive a smooth surrogate from the unique root of a smooth threshold equation. Implicit differentiation gives closed-form derivatives with normalised local weights, whose distribution is controlled by a smoothing parameter. These derivatives are used in a straight-through procedure: the forward pass evaluates the exact rank filter, while the backward pass uses the surrogate. For fixed ranks, the procedure learns real-valued structuring elements of any rank filter, including the median, and extends to compositions, infima, and suprema of rank filters. In image denoising, our best network also outperforms smooth morphological networks in all settings. On vessel segmentation, the learned erosions recover structuring elements that fit the vessels, as theoretically expected, whereas most of those trained with exact subgradients remain close to their initialisation.

☆ DS-BiCA-Net: Pair-Preserving Cross-Temporal Modeling for Remote Sensing Change Captioning
Licheng Zhang, Naveed Akhtar, Siew-Kei Lam
Remote sensing image change captioning (RSICC) describes in natural language the semantic changes between two images of the same scene captured at different times. Previous methods commonly merge the pair during repeated processing or combine intra-image and cross-image relations in one operation, weakening source identity and leaving the two temporal directions implicit. Without separate modules for intra-image and cross-temporal processing and a separate path for each direction, the contribution of each part cannot be measured on its own, so it remains unclear which part matters most, and the design of later models has no such evidence to build on. To address these issues, we propose DS-BiCA-Net, which assigns the two kinds of processing to separate modules and keeps the two images as separate streams throughout the encoder. A windowed state-space module models context within each image, and a bidirectional cross-attention module compares the two images along two directed paths that share their projections. The two modules use the same pre-normalisation residual architecture and differ only in their mixers, and the two streams are fused only in the aggregation head, so each module and each direction can be removed and its contribution measured on its own. Controlled experiments on LEVIR-CC and Dubai-CC examine operator interaction, temporal direction and module order, showing that intra-image refinement carries no benefit alone and becomes beneficial only when followed by bidirectional cross-attention, an order that outperforms the reverse at matched parameter count and FLOPs. The bidirectional module also outperforms either temporal direction alone. Our method reaches an S_m^* of 82.65 on LEVIR-CC, the highest among the published results compared, and 66.72 on Dubai-CC without geometric augmentation, the second-highest among the published results compared.

Vision-Language Models (VLMs) are widely deployed, yet the internal mechanisms behind their safety behavior remain poorly understood. We present a lightweight inference-time framework for localizing and manipulating safety-sensitive representations in frozen VLMs, without retraining or modifying parameters. On Qwen3-VL-4B, layer-wise activation divergence analysis reveals non-uniform safety geometry across depth. Causal interventions show that early vision layers support strong bidirectional refusal control through activation steering along a learned safety direction, with unsafe rejection spanning 6%-96%, whereas later layers respond more to activation magnitude scaling and exhibit a substantial safety-selectivity trade-off. Deeper layers remain well separated along the safety direction yet are largely insensitive to steering, distinguishing representational separability from causal controllability. InternVL2.5-4B shows qualitatively similar depth-dependent activation geometry despite differences in layer location and magnitude. Our results expose a white-box, representation-level refusal-bypass attack surface in VLM vision encoders and motivate inference-time stabilization of safety-sensitive representations.

Achieving this flexibility is a major open challenge in AI: capabilities often remain separated across specialized models, limiting how they can be composed and jointly adapted to a task. We introduce $Ψ$-0.6, a unified vision-language world model that adaptively composes perception, language, geometry, and simulation within a shared reasoning process we call streams of thought. ☆ Forging Emotions: a deep learning experiment on emotions and art
Amalia Foka
Affective computing is an interdisciplinary field that studies computational methods that relate to or influence emotion. These methods have been applied to interactive media artworks, but they have focused on affect detection rather than affect generation. For affect generation, computationally creative methods need to be explored that have recently been driven by the use of Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs), a deep learning method. The experiment presented in this paper, Forging Emotions, explores the use of visual emotion datasets and the working processes of GANs for visual affect generation, that is, for generating images that can convey or trigger specified emotions. This experiment concludes that the methodology used so far by computer science researchers to build image datasets for describing high-level concepts such as emotions is insufficient and proposes utilizing emotional networks of associations according to psychology research. Forging Emotions also concludes that to generate affect visually, merely corresponding to basic psychology findings, such as bright or dark colours, does not seem adequate. Therefore, research efforts should aim to understand the structure of trained GANs and compositional GANs in order to produce genuinely novel compositions that can convey or trigger emotions through the subject matter of generated images.

☆ Playing Bias: Epistemic Games for Interpreting Text-to-Image Models
Amalia Foka
Text-to-image (T2I) systems do not merely render prompts; they circulate defaults for "what X looks like," shaping recognition through pose, camera, costume, props, and setting. While technical audits quantify disparities, they rarely cultivate the literacy needed to argue how images assemble stereotypes and confer authority. This paper translates a three-stage, humanities-informed framework into a set of epistemic games that make this cultural work visible and debatable: Interpret (art-historical close looking with AI outputs), Interrogate (counter-intent prompting as artistic exploration), and Expose (creative misuse through paired prompts with a constant motif and a BiasSlot rule, in which only the bias cue varies). In a pilot with undergraduate fine-arts students, the games shifted discussion from impressionistic reactions to concise, warranted hypotheses grounded in visual evidence, supported by lightweight classroom instruments that enabled reproducibility and structured collaboration. We argue that such game-based approaches foster critical literacy across educational contexts, equipping learners to recognize, discuss, and contest how T2I models encode bias.

Existing vision-language and keyword-based retrieval methods often miss these events because the relevant motion may not be explicitly described in text or captured by lexical overlap. We further introduce a look-ahead mechanism to refine resampled particles before weighting. The low-entropy requirement concerns identity uncertainty, while appearance may remain diverse. We formulate identity fidelity in terms of the probability that a conditional image distribution assigns to the identities permitted by the prompt. Visual Identity Spaces (VIS) formalize this distinction by specifying admissible identity values and which different realizations express the same identity. We test at scale on public benchmarks. On VSI-Bench ($288$ videos, $5{,}130$ questions) SpatialMem scores $37.5$ overall with RGB alone, and its margin is precisely where a metric memory should earn it (room size $41.4$ vs.\ $24.4$ with a same-size frame model). On the episodic-memory task of OpenEQA ($953$ questions) the memory serialised to text is lower than the blind control, but as evidence-frame retrieval it recovers frame-level accuracy, matching uniform sampling at an equal eight-frame budget and pulling ahead as the budget tightens, with every answer grounded in linked 3D evidence. On $12$ ScanNet scenes evaluated using instance-level official annotations, the anchor-first hierarchy assigns the retrieved object to the proper structural parent where open-vocabulary 3D scene graphs essentially cannot ($0.24$ compared to $0.01$ with matched input), a capability difference instead of an overall win. The queryable index has a cost of $14$\,KB per scene without the linked evidence frames, and we make available the suites, memories and code.
♻ ☆ Velocity-Space 3D Asset Editing NeurIPS 2026
Hao Liu, Yuxuan Lin, Jingfeng Guo, Ruihang Chu, Junjie Wang, Ruotong Li, Yujiu Yang
Local 3D asset editing requires modifying a target region while preserving the rest. Existing methods enforce locality through mechanisms external to the generator, such as manual 3D masks, post-hoc voxel merging, or 2D multi-view lifting. None intervene where the corruption originates: inside the ODE sampler. For faithful local editing, a rectified-flow generator's velocity field should be strong over the target region while vanishing on preserved content. Yet a single velocity field can hardly satisfy both requirements, leading to three problems: (i) identity leakage that keeps the edit signal non-zero on preserved regions; (ii) no dedicated edit-amplification channel, so strengthening the edit perturbs identity; and (iii) identity drag at the geometry and material stages, where a global condition pulls every token toward the target. We propose VS3D (Velocity-Space 3D Asset editing), an inversion-free, training-free, and mask-free framework that derives edit and preserve signals by comparing the frozen model's source- and target-conditioned responses and realizes this principle through three stage-specific modules. Reconstruction-Anchored Source Injection (RASI) absorbs identity leakage by turning the unconditional embedding into a per-step, asset-specific anchor calibrated through source reconstruction. Partial-Mean Guidance (PMG) amplifies the edit signal by contrasting high- and low-quality subsample estimates of the velocity difference, active only where a consistent edit exists. Twin-Agreement Residual Injection (TAR) lets the sampler decide token by token what to preserve at the geometry and material stages. Experiments on diverse 3D assets show that VS3D outperforms state-of-the-art native-3D and 2D-lifted editors, demonstrating the effectiveness of velocity-space editing for training-free 3D asset editing. Code is publicly available at https://github.com/LHaoooo/VS3D.
comment: Accepted at NeurIPS 2026. Revised manuscript with additional experiments and supplementary material
♻ ☆ Order Matters: Competition-Guided Query Ordering for RNN-Based Object Detection NeurIPS 2026
Shengjian Wu, Li Sun, Yu Shangguan, Qingli Li
DETR-style detectors use one-to-one bipartite matching during training to assign object queries to ground-truth objects, enabling end-to-end set prediction without non-maximum suppression (NMS). However, without an explicit de-duplication procedure, multiple queries can still produce highly similar hypotheses for the same object, making training unstable and predictions less decisive. Inspired by the sequential ordering of NMS, we propose DETRNN, a plug-and-play module that turns unordered object queries into a competition-aware sequence for recurrent refinement. DETRNN builds an explicit confidence-and-similarity based order from prior predictions, then refines queries with an RNN along this order to model competition inside the decoder. This ordered recurrent refinement reduces redundant predictions, stabilizes optimization, and improves final detection accuracy. Experiments on multiple DETR-style detectors show consistent gains with comparable efficiency. Code repository: https://github.com/nigelwoo2008-coder/DETRNN.
comment: Accepted at NeurIPS 2026
♻ ☆ StemBind: When MLLMs Get Lost Between Rules and Instances in Abstract Visual Reasoning NeurIPS 2026
Xixiang He, Baiqi Wu, Xingming Li, Ao Cheng, Qiyao Sun, Xuanyu Ji, Qingyong Hu
Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) often know the rule but pick the wrong answer: on abstract visual reasoning (AVR) tasks, a model can describe what it sees and name the underlying pattern, yet still fail to choose the matching candidate. Existing AVR benchmarks cannot detect this because they collapse perception, rule induction, and answer selection into a single right-or-wrong signal. We introduce StemBind, a shared-stem diagnostic benchmark that probes the same visual stem with three aligned questions: Perception (what is in the image), Rule (what pattern governs it), and Full (which option completes it), so a final-answer error can be attributed to a specific sub-step on the same evidence. StemBind contains 2,298 curated knowledge-light stems across nine auditable visual operations, totaling 19,533 P/R/F tasks, with each full item annotated by Sternberg's four reasoning stages (S1 Encode, S2 Infer, S3 Map, S4 Apply). Evaluating 24 frontier MLLM configurations yields four findings. (i) The R-F chasm: rule accuracy exceeds full-item accuracy on 22 of 24 models, so most failures happen after the rule is identified. (ii) A persistent binding gap: even when P and R are both correct on the same stem, models still answer F incorrectly 51.2% of the time. (iii) The bottleneck is S3: process diagnostics and Stage-wise Stimulus Augmentation localize the dominant failure to rule-to-instance mapping. (iv) Scaling and thinking do not help: neither larger models nor explicit thinking mode reliably closes the gap, and thinking even lowers rule and full-item accuracy. StemBind reframes AVR evaluation from final-answer ranking to locating where abstract visual reasoning breaks down, identifying rule-to-instance binding as a concrete next target for vision-grounded reasoning.
comment: Accepted at NeurIPS 2026 (Evaluations and Datasets Track). Camera-ready version. Project page: https://hexixiang.github.io/StemBind ; Code: https://github.com/hexixiang/StemBind ; Data: https://huggingface.co/datasets/user48271/Stembind
♻ ☆ Attractive Faces Skew Text-to-Image Reward Models and Leaderboards
Harvey Mannering, Zhiwu Huang, Adam Prügel-Bennett
Human preference is now central to the evaluation, guidance, finetuning, and ranking of text-to-image models. However, the susceptibility of human preferences to bias in image generation remains underexplored. We identify a key observation: for human faces, perceived attractiveness overrides image quality in preference judgments, even when comparing real photographs of comparable fidelity. In a controlled user study, annotators rank more attractive faces as higher quality, even when unattractive real faces are compared with attractive AI-generated ones. We examine the downstream consequences of this bias. Firstly, simulating Elo rankings from user study data shows attractiveness can distort a leaderboard's ranking, elevating synthetic attractive faces over real, unattractive ones. Secondly, the same bias reappears in the human preference models. Editing 40 annotated facial attributes in isolation, we find that attractiveness is the strongest correlate of score for four of five human preference models (PickScore, MPS, HPSv2.1, HPSv3), and the strongest predictor of score in regression analysis. We further show that preference aligned generation shifts faces toward younger, more feminine faces, and can override explicit prompts for unattractive faces, thereby limiting user control. Finally, we explore mitigation strategies, both for data collection and post training on human preference models. These findings highlight the need for preference models that disentangle image quality from human cognitive bias, enabling more reliable evaluation.
comment: WACV 2027
♻ ☆ Half-Truths Break Similarity-Based Retrieval NeurIPS 2026
Bora Kargi, Arnas Uselis, Seong Joon Oh
When a text description is extended with an additional detail, image-text similarity should drop if that detail is wrong. We show that CLIP-style dual encoders often violate this intuition: appending a plausible but incorrect object or relation to an otherwise correct description can increase the similarity score. We call such cases half-truths. On COCO, CLIP prefers the correct shorter description only 34.0% of the time, and performance drops to 27.8% when the added detail is a relation. We trace this vulnerability to weak supervision on caption parts: contrastive training aligns full sentences but does not explicitly enforce that individual entities and relations are grounded. We propose CS-CLIP (Component-Supervised CLIP), which decomposes captions into entity and relation units, constructs a minimally edited foil for each unit, and fine-tunes the model to score the correct unit above its foil while preserving standard dual-encoder inference. CS-CLIP raises half-truth accuracy to 76.4% and improves average performance on established compositional benchmarks by 5.8 points, suggesting that reducing half-truth errors aligns with broader gains in compositional understanding.
comment: Accepted at NeurIPS 2026. Camera-ready version with expanded evaluation and additional analyses. 40 pages, 10 figures, including appendices. Code, checkpoints, and datasets: https://github.com/kargibora/CS-CLIP
♻ ☆ Barycentric Guidance: Turning Foundation Image Editors into Continuous Affective Controllers NeurIPS 2026
Harvey Mannering, Zhiwu Huang, Adam Prügel-Bennett
Emotions are expressed on a continuum and are naturally described in the valence-arousal (VA) space. Existing VA-based image editors are typically training-based and domain-specific, limiting them to VA regions seen during training and making them brittle across datasets and domains. Meanwhile, despite producing high-quality edits, state-of-the-art foundation image editors are not continuous affective controllers: non-linear emotion representations in text encoders makes prompt interpolation poorly calibrated, so accurate and continuous VA control remains unreliable. To fill this gap, we introduce Barycentric Guidance, a training-free framework that turns pretrained foundation image editors into continuous affective controllers over VA, requiring no finetuning, extra data, or model changes. Our method maps any target VA point to simplex-based guidance weights, enabling VA controllability in three aspects: (i) accurate targeting of VA states, (ii) broad coverage across the VA plane, and (iii) continuous control. Across three face datasets, we improve VA target accuracy by 25-29%, expand VA-plane coverage by 28-50%, and increase expression diversity by 29-49%, over the strongest baseline. Unlike prior domain-specific methods, our training-free approach exploits the foundation model's inherent versatility, enabling generalization beyond human faces to animals, artworks, and complex scenes within a single framework. Code is available at https://github.com/harveymannering/BarycentricGuidance.
comment: NeurIPS 2026
♻ ☆ Localization and Neural Splatting on the Edge: An FPGA Scene Memory for Robots
Haohua Que, Mingkai Liu, Tianle Zhu, Handong Yao
Resource-constrained robots and autonomous vehicles need scene memories that localize a camera and render nearby views without a desktop GPU. Scene-coordinate regression (SCR) and 3D Gaussian splatting (3DGS) fit because they avoid an SfM stage, but ACEsplat-style pipelines are GPU-centered, and moving them to an edge FPGA is hard because SCR is pose-sensitive and 3DGS rendering is irregular and capacity-sensitive. We present LENS, an edge scene-memory acceleration system on the AMD KR260 that brings an ACEsplat-style workload to a low-power FPGA/ARM platform. Rather than proposing a new scene model, LENS co-designs the two dominant kernels with the board data path: an INT16 SCR accelerator that preserves pose accuracy, and a bit-exact fixed-point ordered 3DGS renderer that rewrites alpha transmittance as a log-sum-exp recurrence and removes provably useless streamed Gaussians. All LENS latency, power, and quality results are board-measured. The SCR engine preserves DSAC* localization accuracy at 25.42 ms, the on-board renderer reaches 34.11 dB on Cambridge against ACEsplat's 33.20, novel-view synthesis on RealEstate10K reaches 27.84 dB against 26.11, and all ten Wayspots scenes reach the ACEsplat rendering target. LENS wins performance per watt over a Jetson Orin NX on every deployment task, by 1.9x to 5.7x at about a quarter of the power, and is faster in absolute latency on localization and Wayspots rendering. On-device training reaches ACEsplat-level quality but not the GPU's time or energy, marking the remaining boundary for a future training accelerator.
comment: 8 pages
♻ ☆ OccamView: Object-Conditioned View Selection for Frame-Budgeted Active 3D Gaussian Reconstruction
Hongbo Gao, Wei Zhang, Zeyu Ni, Dihao Zhu, Ruifeng Li, Yunke Wang, Chang Xu
Active 3D Gaussian reconstruction fundamentally relies on selecting informative next-best views under limited sensing budgets. Existing active 3DGS methods primarily plan viewpoints according to geometric information gain, treating object-induced hidden regions in the same manner as general unexplored space. Under tight frame budgets, such geometry-driven strategies may prioritize global scene coverage while leaving partially observed objects incompletely reconstructed. To address this limitation, we propose OccamView, an object-conditioned view-selection framework for frame-budgeted active 3D Gaussian reconstruction. Rather than predicting unseen object geometry or performing shape completion, OccamView maintains an online object memory from open-vocabulary detections grounded in measured RGB-D observations and represents unresolved local occupancy around detected objects as conservative hidden-region proxies. Candidate viewpoints are then evaluated using an occlusion-aware proxy-coverage score. Furthermore, we introduce a Geo-Floor mechanism that restricts object-conditioned re-ranking to geometrically competitive candidates, allowing object-conditioned cues to guide complementary observations while preserving the geometry-driven exploration behavior of the underlying planner. Experiments on Replica and Matterport3D under a unified frame-budgeted protocol show that OccamView consistently reduces Completion and improves Completion Ratio across five frame budgets, with particularly pronounced gains under limited frame budgets. These results demonstrate that lightweight object-conditioned cues effectively complement geometry-driven active view planning.
